meta.title: Burn ICU Case Study: Marcus Delaney, a Three-Day ICU Stay, Shift by Shift
meta.footer: Write one answer per numbered box, inside the box, in dark pen, neatly. Open book, individual work.

lines: You are the Burn ICU nurse for Marcus Delaney, a 34-year-old man in room BICU-6 with burns from a house fire. Open the patient in the student EHR (Student View, or the patient file from your instructor). He arrived in the ICU at 0400 on Monday 11/02/26 and the night nurse has cared for him since. You take over at the 0700 shift change, and the chart runs until his transfer to a medical-surgical unit on Thursday 11/05/26 at 0700.

You will work through his stay one 12-hour shift at a time. At the start of each shift, set the simulation clock to the time written at the top of that shift and read the chart up to that moment. You may not need to look past the end of the shift you are working on. Each question tells you where to look in the EHR.
Shift 1: Monday 11/02, 0700 to 1900 (day).   Shift 2: Monday 1900 to Tuesday 11/03 0700 (night).   Shift 3: Tuesday 0700 to 1900 (day).
Shift 4: Tuesday 1900 to Wednesday 11/04 0700 (night).   Shift 5: Wednesday 0700 to 1900 (day).   Shift 6: Wednesday 1900 to Thursday 11/05 0700 (night, ends with transfer to Med-Surg).

Each numbered question is a real nursing decision or a piece of reasoning you would do on the unit: reading the flowsheets, labs, orders, MAR and notes, doing the math, and explaining what you would do and why. Write your answer in the large box under each question. Short, specific answers that use Marcus's own numbers earn more points than general textbook answers.
Expect to spend about one hour on each shift, six hours in all. It is a take-home, individual, open-book assignment: use your textbooks, drug guide, notes and the chart.
The whole case study is worth 100 points. A score of 78 or higher is passing.
Each numbered question shows its point value. Points are given only for what is written in the box.

studentRules.h: Writing and turning it in (your pages will be scanned)
lines: Write in dark pen or very dark pencil, print clearly, and stay inside the box. Write the answer in the box with the same number as the question.
Write your name and date at the top of every page (the header prints a line for it).
If you need more room, write "continued on the back" and put the question number on the back.
Spell out drug names. Show your math: write the formula, the numbers and the units.
Do not take photos of your work. Your instructor will scan it.
TURN-IN: put ALL the pages in order and fasten them with a PAPERCLIP. Do NOT staple (the pages must come apart to be scanned). Leave the packet in the instructor's cubby at office G218i.

keyIntro.h: How to score (applies to every item)
lines: Score only what is written in the student's box. Spelling and grammar are not scored. Accept equivalent wording and correct synonyms. Give each element once.
Partial points: use the amounts printed beside each element. Round the item total to the nearest 0.5. An item never earns more than its maximum.
If a box is illegible or blank, give 0 and list the item on the score sheet under "faculty review."
Chart answers are judged against the chart at the time written in the question. Small differences in totals read from the EHR (plus or minus 50 mL) are acceptable.

Marcus Delaney, 34, 82 kg, 180 cm. House fire at 0130 Monday. Flame burn 22% TBSA (right arm circumferential, anterior chest, face and neck; about 8% full thickness) with smoke inhalation (COHb 14.2%), intubated at 0250, right forearm/hand escharotomy at 0315, Burn ICU arrival 0400.

Parkland: 4 mL x 82 kg x 22% = 7,216 mL lactated Ringer's in 24 hours from the time of injury. Day 2 (Tuesday) he develops burn wound sepsis (MSSA), needs norepinephrine, and improves overnight; he is extubated Wednesday 1045 and transfers Thursday 0700.
All six shifts are written. The point total is 100: Shift 1 = 20 (it includes the admission picture and the handoff), Shifts 2 to 6 = 16 each.

parts.title: Shift 1: Monday 11/02, 0700 to 1900 (day shift)
parts.intro: Set the simulation clock to 0700 on Monday 11/02/26 and move it forward as you work. Marcus arrived in the ICU at 0400; you take report from the night nurse and care for him until you hand off at 1900. You can read everything charted before 0700, and the chart fills in as the clock moves forward.
parts.keyNote: Shift 1 is mostly chart reading and the safety reasoning behind burn resuscitation. A careful student should earn about 16 of the 20 points. The hardest items are 1.2 (the Parkland math with the EMS bolus) and 1.10 (the fluid totals).

items.title: Why Is He Here? Your Picture of Marcus at 0700
items.prompt: Set the clock to 0700. You are taking report from the night nurse. Read the ED Provider Note, the Burn Surgery and Critical Care H&Ps, the nursing notes from 0425 to 0650 and the Patient Summary. In your own words, explain what happened to Marcus, what injuries he has and what has already been done, then name the THREE most urgent problems you must manage over the next 12 hours.
items.where: Patient Summary; Chart Review > Notes (ED Provider Note, Burn Surgery H&P, Critical Care H&P, Nursing Admission Note)

elements.t: Mechanism and burn: house fire about 0130 Mon, flame burns 22% TBSA (right arm circumferential, anterior chest, face/neck), about 8% full thickness (right forearm and hand).
Inhalation injury and carbon monoxide: hoarse voice, stridor, soot, singed nasal hairs; COHb 14.2% at 0250; intubated 0250; bronchoscopy shows grade 2 inhalation injury.
Right forearm/hand escharotomy at 0315 (tense forearm, no Doppler signal) with pulses returned.

Burn shock resuscitation: Parkland lactated Ringer's started at 450 mL/h and titrated to urine output (raised to 540 mL/h at 0600 for urine output of 25 and 26 mL/h); lactate 5.8 at 0250 down to 3.4 at 0415 (the 0800 result comes later).
Ventilated and sedated (propofol, fentanyl); lines/tubes: left IJ central line, left radial arterial line, OG tube, Foley with temperature probe.

Three priorities that make sense, for example: (1) airway/ventilation and carbon monoxide; (2) fluid resuscitation titrated to urine output; (3) circulation to the right hand after escharotomy (also acceptable: pain/sedation, infection prevention).

items.title: The Parkland Formula
items.prompt: Find the burn size and his weight in the chart. (a) Calculate his total 24-hour fluid need with the Parkland formula. (b) How much must he receive in the FIRST 8 hours, and by what clock time does that period end? (c) EMS gave 500 mL of lactated Ringer's before the ED. Explain how that changes the hourly rate for the first 8 hours, counting from his ED arrival at 0230. (d) What rate is the second half of the fluid given at? Show your work with the units. Why is the clock started at the time of the injury and not at his arrival?
items.where: Patient Summary (weight); Burn Surgery H&P (TBSA); Orders (lactated Ringer's); EMS Handoff Summary

elements.t: Total: 4 mL x 82 kg x 22 = 7,216 mL lactated Ringer's in 24 hours (0.25 formula, 0.25 answer).
First half = 3,608 mL in the first 8 hours from the INJURY (0130 to 0930).
Subtract the EMS 500 mL: 3,108 mL over the 7 hours from 0230 to 0930 = about 444 mL/h (accept 450 mL/h, which matches the order).
Second half = 3,608 mL over the next 16 hours (0930 to 0130 Tue) = 225 mL/h.
The clock starts at the injury because the capillary leak and fluid loss begin then; the first hours are the most critical (any equivalent reason).

items.title: Vital Sign Trend
items.where: Flowsheets > Vital Signs
items.prompt: Copy the vital signs at each time (he has an arterial line, so use the blood pressure shown). Circle every abnormal value. Then, in one or two sentences, describe the trend over the shift and say which value on the flowsheet you do NOT fully trust and why.

key.rules: Score 1.0 x (cells correct / 24), rounded to the nearest 0.5. The trend sentence is worth 0.5: heart rate starts high (111) and falls to 97 as the resuscitation works; blood pressure is low-normal (99/57 to 109/63, MAP about 71 to 78); temperature rises from 98.2 F to 99.2 F (he arrived cold at 96.8 F); CPOT stays 1 because he is sedated. The value NOT to trust fully is the SpO2 of 98-99%: carbon monoxide on the hemoglobin makes the pulse oximeter read falsely normal. Allow +/- 2 for rates and +/- 0.2 F. Abnormal values to circle: heart rate above 100 (111, 104, 102), and temperature, blood pressure and CPOT may be circled or not if the student explains why (accept reasonable choices).

items.title: Trend (scored with 1.3)
items.prompt: Describe the trend over the shift and name the value you do NOT fully trust and why.

items.title: The Pulse Oximeter Says 100%
items.prompt: Marcus's SpO2 reads 99 to 100% all morning. (a) Explain why this number can be falsely reassuring in this patient. (b) Which lab results show how much carbon monoxide is on his hemoglobin, and what were the values at 0250, 0415 and 0800? (c) What treatment lowers it, and what did the night team change at 0600 (read their notes)? (d) He smokes a pack a day: what does that tell you about the value he is heading toward?
items.where: Lab Results > Blood Gas (Carboxyhemoglobin, PaO2); Orders (ventilator); Flowsheets > Respiratory

elements.t: A pulse oximeter cannot tell carboxyhemoglobin from oxyhemoglobin, so it reads normal even though the blood carries much less oxygen.
Carboxyhemoglobin (co-oximetry on the arterial blood gas): 14.2% at 0250, 6.4% at 0415, 3.1% at 0800.

100% oxygen (FiO2 1.0 through the ventilator) shortens the half-life of carbon monoxide; FiO2 was weaned from 1.0 to 0.60 at 0600 as the level fell (6.4% at 0415), with a repeat level at 0800 before weaning further (FiO2 0.50 at 1400).

A heavy smoker normally runs a COHb of roughly 3 to 10% (accept 3 to 5% or higher), so a level around 3% is at his baseline and not further poisoning; the level is heading down to his smoker baseline, not to zero.

items.title: Titrating the Fluids
items.prompt: Open the lactated Ringer's order, the MAR and the hourly urine output. (a) What is the urine output goal in mL/h and in mL/kg/h? (b) At 0930 the rate was changed: from what to what, and why? (c) Using the graph, write the urine outputs for 1200-1300 and 1300-1400, say what the order tells you to do, and what the new rate becomes at 1400. (d) Name two things you check when you change the rate and one danger of giving too much fluid.
items.where: Orders > lactated Ringer's (burn resuscitation); MAR (rate changes); Flowsheets > Intake/Output

images.caption: EHR screenshot: Orders, order detail for the lactated Ringer's (click the order to open this panel).
EHR screenshot: the MAR row for the lactated Ringer's on Monday (rate changes are shown in the hour they happened).
Graph from the chart: hourly urine output (bars, shaded band is the goal) and the lactated Ringer's rate (line), Monday 0400 to 1900.

elements.t: Goal 30 to 50 mL/h, which is 0.5 mL/kg/h (about 41 mL/h for 82 kg).
At 0930 (8 hours after the injury) the first half of the Parkland fluid is done, so the rate dropped from 540 to 225 mL/h for the second 16 hours.
Urine output 28 mL and 28 mL: below 30 mL/h for two hours in a row, so increase the rate by 20 to 25% and notify the burn team.

Two checks (lung sounds / peak airway pressures, abdomen or bladder pressure, right hand pulses and tension, edema, blood pressure, heart rate) AND a danger of too much fluid ("fluid creep": pulmonary edema, compartment syndrome, more ventilator days, worse swelling).

items.title: Calling the Burn Surgeon
items.prompt: It is 1400 and you have just seen the second low urine output. Write the SBAR you give Dr. Okafor on the phone. Use real numbers from the chart. End with what you are asking him to do and how you will confirm the order.
items.where: Flowsheets (vital signs, I&O, neurovascular); Lab Results (lactate, potassium, CK); Orders

elements.t: Situation: identify yourself, the patient and room; urine output 28 mL/h and 28 mL/h for two hours (about 0.34 mL/kg/h, less than the goal of 0.5) on lactated Ringer's 225 mL/h.
Background: 34-year-old, 82 kg, 22% TBSA flame burn with inhalation injury, intubated and sedated, on the Parkland resuscitation since 0230, EMS 500 mL, escharotomy right arm.

Assessment: current vitals at 1400 (T 99.0, HR 102, BP 108/63 with MAP 78, SpO2 99%; accept the 1300 values HR 103, BP 105/61), lungs/peak pressures (PIP 27, Pplat 20), bladder pressure 12 mmHg, right hand Doppler pulses, lactate normal at 1.8 (1200), CK 1,120, and your concern that he is behind on fluid.
Recommendation: ask to increase the rate by 20% per the order (to 270 mL/h) and what urine output you should call about next; read the order back and document the time and name.

items.title: Lines, Tubes and Airway
items.prompt: List SIX lines, tubes or devices Marcus has at 0700 (not counting the ventilator). For each, write the site and what you check every shift, and one complication you are watching for.
items.where: Avatar (IVs, drains and tubes); Flowsheets > Lines / Drains / Airways; Nursing Admission Note

images.caption: EHR screenshot: the Patient Summary page, Avatar and Active Devices list at 0700 (scroll the list to see every device).

cols: What you check or do every shift

key.answer: Each device row is worth 0.25: the device and site are right AND the check/complication fit that device.

elements.t: Endotracheal tube, 8.0 oral, 24 cm at the teeth: confirm depth and securement, cuff pressure (about 24), HOB 30, oral care, suction as needed. Complications: accidental extubation, VAP, pressure injury to the lips, tube obstruction.
Left internal jugular central line (triple lumen): chlorhexidine dressing intact, scrub the hub, daily need review, label lumens. Complications: infection (CLABSI), air embolism, clot, bleeding.
Left radial arterial line (right arm is burned): waveform, level and zero, check the left hand circulation, pressure bag 300 mmHg. Complications: hand ischemia, bleeding or disconnection, infection.
OG tube 16 Fr: position confirmed by x-ray, mark at the lips, residual and feeds per order, HOB 30. Complications: aspiration, misplacement, intolerance (residual, distention).

Foley catheter 16 Fr with temperature probe: hourly output, secured, closed system, catheter care. Complications: CAUTI, kinks/low output that is really a blocked catheter, bladder pressure reading for compartment syndrome.
Left antecubital 18 g peripheral IV: site check, flush, patency. Complications: infiltration, phlebitis, infection. (Also accept the escharotomy sites on the right arm as a device row.)

items.title: The Ventilator and Sedation
items.prompt: Open Flowsheets > Respiratory at 0700. (a) Calculate his ideal body weight (male: 50 kg + 2.3 kg for every inch over 5 feet; 1 inch = 2.54 cm) and the tidal volume at 6 mL/kg. Does this match the set tidal volume? (b) List FOUR actions in the ventilator-associated pneumonia (VAP) bundle that you do this shift. (c) What is the RASS goal on Monday, and why is he sedated more deeply on the first day?
items.where: Flowsheets > Respiratory (vent settings, pressures); Orders (mechanical ventilation; sedation); Orders > Nursing

elements.t: 180 cm = 70.9 inches, so IBW = 50 + 2.3 x 10.9 = about 75 kg; 6 mL/kg = about 450 mL. The set tidal volume is 450 mL, which matches (accept 75-76 kg and 450-455 mL).

Any four VAP bundle actions: head of bed 30 degrees or higher, oral care with chlorhexidine every 12 h, daily sedation interruption and spontaneous breathing trial, cuff pressure check, suction only when needed, stress ulcer and DVT prophylaxis, hand hygiene (0.125 each).
RASS goal -2 to -3 on Monday; deeper sedation and analgesia are needed on day 1 for painful burn care, resuscitation, the airway swelling and the risk of pulling the tube.

items.title: Reading the Labs
items.prompt: Open Lab Results and compare the first draws (about 0240-0250) with the 1200 and 1800 draws. Choose FOUR labs or lab groups that changed or matter. For each, write the values, why this happens in a burn patient, and what you do about it.
items.where: Lab Results (Chemistry, CBC, Blood Gas)
cols: Lab and values (first draw to latest)

key.answer: Any 4 of the labs below; each row 0.375: values correct (0.125), reason correct (0.125), nursing action reasonable (0.125).

elements.t: Lactate 5.8 -> 3.4 -> 2.2 -> 1.8 -> 1.6 (critical to normal): poor tissue perfusion early; falling means the fluid resuscitation is working. Keep trending; a rise means shock or sepsis, notify.
Hemoglobin 17.2 -> 13.6 (and hematocrit 51 -> 41): hemoconcentration from plasma leak on arrival, then dilution as fluid is given. Watch for bleeding and new drops.
CK 480 -> 1,120: muscle and tissue injury; protect the kidneys with adequate urine output and watch for dark urine (myoglobin); report the trend.

Potassium 4.3 -> 4.5 -> 4.9 -> 5.0: cells release potassium after burn injury; monitor the ECG and recheck; do not replace it, and report the rising trend to the provider (no call value is written in the orders, so accept asking the provider for one).
WBC 12.8 -> 16.1 (1200): stress response to a major burn, NOT an infection yet; use it as a baseline for comparison later.
Glucose 143 -> 156 -> 172 -> 188 (serum): stress hyperglycemia that keeps rising; check glucose per order and know the call parameters, because an insulin infusion is likely if it stays above 180.
pH 7.29 -> 7.39 (7.40 at 1600) and bicarbonate 18 -> 24 (arterial gas): metabolic acidosis from poor perfusion corrected with resuscitation.
Carboxyhemoglobin 14.2 -> 3.0 (also accept if not used in 1.4).

items.title: Adding Up Your 12 Hours
items.prompt: Open Flowsheets > Intake/Output and find the Totals section at the bottom (the screenshot shows where). (a) For the DAY SHIFT 0700 to 1900, what are his total intake, total output and net balance? (b) What was his average urine output in mL/h and in mL/kg/h (82 kg)? (c) Using the Parkland rates, how much lactated Ringer's should he have received BY 1900 counting from the injury (the EMS 500 mL and the ED 675 mL before the ICU count), and how much did he actually receive in all (add up the rates and times on the MAR)? (d) What does that tell you?
items.where: Flowsheets > Intake/Output (Totals at the bottom); MAR (lactated Ringer's); EMS Handoff and ED notes

images.caption: EHR screenshot: the Totals section at the bottom of the Intake/Output flowsheet, at 1900 on Monday.

elements.t: Day shift 0700-1900 as the flowsheet shows it: intake 4,720 mL, output 447 mL, net +4,273 mL (a large positive balance is expected in burn resuscitation). Use the displayed totals; a student who adds the hourly columns by hand may get slightly different numbers (accept if the method is sound).
Average urine output 447 / 12 = about 37 mL/h = about 0.45 mL/kg/h (accept 37-38 mL/h and 0.45-0.47; just under the 0.5 goal, inside 30-50 mL/h most of the shift).

Expected by 1900: first 8 h = 3,608 mL plus 9.5 h x 225 = about 2,140 mL, about 5,750 mL. Actual crystalloid from the MAR: EMS 500 + ED 675 + ICU (450 x 2 h + 540 x 3.5 h + 225 x 4.5 h + 270 x 5 h = 5,153) = about 6,330 mL (accept 6,200-6,350; the progress notes quote about 6,190 at 1800 and 6,280 at 1850 with their own rounding).

He is about 580 mL (10%) over the Parkland estimate: acceptable because the order is to titrate to urine output, but a reminder to watch for fluid creep (edema, airway pressures, bladder pressure) and not to chase a single low urine output.

items.title: The 1400 Dressing Change
items.prompt: Read the Burn Wound Assessment note and the 1520 nursing note. (a) Why was hydromorphone given at 1345 and what tool measures pain in an intubated, sedated patient (name its four parts)? (b) Which topical drugs were applied and where? (c) What do you assess at every dressing change? (d) Name two ways you protect him and yourself from infection.
items.where: Chart Review > Notes (Burn Wound Assessment; Nursing Note 1520); MAR (hydromorphone, silver sulfadiazine, bacitracin)

elements.t: Dressing changes are the most painful part of burn care; the opioid is given about 15 minutes BEFORE the procedure so it is working. CPOT has four parts: facial expression, body movements, muscle tension, compliance with the ventilator.
Silver sulfadiazine 1% cream to the chest and right arm; bacitracin ointment to the face.

Wound color, depth, drainage amount and odor, eschar, blisters, edges and any redness beyond the burn margin (mark and time it), skin around the wound, right hand pulses and capillary refill, and pain response.
Any two: sterile technique, gown/gloves/mask and contact precautions, hand hygiene, dedicated equipment, cleansing the old cream, covering the wound promptly.

items.title: Handoff at 1900
items.prompt: It is 1900. Write your SBAR handoff for E. Haddad, RN, the night nurse. Use real numbers and name what the night nurse must watch for and do in the first part of the night, including anything coming up in the next few hours.
items.where: Everything you have charted and read this shift; Orders; Lab Results; MAR; Flowsheets

elements.t: Situation: patient, room, full code, 22% TBSA burn with inhalation injury, intubated and sedated (propofol and fentanyl), current vitals at 1900 (HR 97, BP 109/63, T 99.2, SpO2 98%; accept the 1800 values HR 98, BP 108/61, T 99.1, SpO2 99%), resuscitation going as planned.

Background: house fire 0130, escharotomy right arm 0315, Parkland (LR 7,216 mL goal in 24 h), lines (central line, arterial line, OG with feeds started at 1000, Foley), COHb down to 3.0% at 1200 (his smoker baseline).

Assessment: urine output was 28 mL/h around 1200-1400 and corrected after the rate went to 270 mL/h (now 42-46 mL/h); net about +4 L; lactate 1.6; potassium 5.0 and glucose 188 are climbing; right hand Doppler pulses steady; pain controlled; wound care done at 1400.

Recommendation / to do: hourly urine output with titration per order; hourly right hand checks; the Parkland 24 hours ends at 0130 Tuesday and the order changes then; 2000 ABG and 0000 labs and CK (glucose may need an insulin infusion if still over 180; recheck potassium); sedation goal and restraint checks; turning and skin care; family visiting; call the burn team for UOP under 20 mL/h.

parts.title: Shift 2: Monday 11/02 1900 to Tuesday 11/03 0700 (night shift)
parts.intro: Set the simulation clock to 1900 on Monday 11/02/26. You take report from the day nurse and care for Marcus until you hand off at 0700. Keep reading forward in the chart as the clock moves; do not look past 0700 for this shift.
parts.keyNote: Shift 2 tests the "quiet" overnight judgment: the end of the Parkland period (1.2 math repeated with the final total), the insulin infusion, an agitation event in a ventilated patient with an alcohol history, and compartment checks. A careful student should earn about 12 of the 16 points.

items.title: Vital Sign Trend Through the Night
items.where: Flowsheets > Vital Signs
items.prompt: Set the clock to 1900 on Monday. You take report from the day nurse. Copy the vital signs at each time, circle every abnormal value, then write two sentences below: what the night looked like overall, and what the flowsheet does NOT show about the agitation event that happened around 0245.

key.rules: Score 1.0 x (cells correct / 24), rounded to the nearest 0.5. The two sentences are worth 0.5: (1) a quiet night: heart rate 93-97 (upper normal, never over 100), BP about 109-111/62-64 (MAP 78-80), temperature 99.2-99.4 F, SpO2 98-99%, CPOT 1; (2) the hourly flowsheet does not show the 0245 agitation: the vital signs at 0300 (HR 93, BP 109/64, SpO2 98%, CPOT 1) look normal and RASS is charted only every 4 hours (-3 at 0000, -2 at 0400), so an event between hourly sets (RASS +1 at 0245, back to -3 by 0315, lorazepam 1 mg at 0300) is recorded only in the nursing note and the MAR. Allow +/- 2 for rates and +/- 0.2 F.

items.title: Overall night, and what the vitals do not show (scored with 2.1)
Glucose and the Insulin Infusion
items.prompt: Open Lab Results (Glucose, point of care and serum), Orders, the MAR and the 0150-0320 nursing notes. (a) List his glucose values from 1800 through 0300 and explain why the insulin infusion was started at 0030 and at what rate. (b) Why does a burn patient have a high glucose even though he has no diabetes? (c) What is the glucose goal and how often do you check it on the infusion? (d) Give TWO safety actions for an insulin infusion, including what you must do if the tube feeding is stopped, and name one lab that you watch closely with insulin.
items.where: Lab Results (Chemistry, Bedside Testing); Orders; MAR (insulin infusion); Chart Review > Notes

elements.t: Glucose: 188 (1800), 198 (2200), 196 (0000), then 191, 190, 189 on the infusion. Started at 1 unit/h at 0030 because the glucose was above 180 on consecutive checks (ICU protocol), ordered by Dr. Brandt.

Stress response of a major burn: stress hormones (cortisol, catecholamines, glucagon) and inflammation make the body insulin resistant and the liver release glucose; the hypermetabolic state and the tube feeding add to it.
Goal 140 to 180 mg/dL; glucose every hour while on the infusion, and adjust the rate per the protocol table.

Any two safety actions: independent double check of the insulin bag and rate (high-alert drug); do not change the rate without the protocol; if feeds are stopped or interrupted, call the provider and recheck the glucose because hypoglycemia is likely (treat glucose under 70 per protocol); dedicated line/label; check glucose after any rate change. AND one lab watched: potassium (insulin moves potassium into cells; K 5.0 at 1800, 4.5 at 0000, 3.9 at 0600).

items.title: The End of the First 24 Hours
items.prompt: The Parkland period ends at 0130 (24 hours after the injury). Using the lactated Ringer's rates and times on the MAR (EMS 500 mL, ED 450 mL/h from 0230 to 0400, then the ICU rates), (a) add up the total crystalloid he received from the injury to 0130 and compare it with the Parkland goal. (b) What did the order change to at 0130 and what new fluid starts at 0600? (c) Why do the fluids not simply stop at 24 hours? (d) His weight was 82 kg on arrival and is now 89.6 kg: what does that tell you and what else do you watch for?
items.where: MAR (lactated Ringer's rate changes); Orders; Flowsheets > Cardiac (daily weight) and Intake/Output; Nursing Note 0150

elements.t: At 0130 lactated Ringer's was lowered to a maintenance rate of 125 mL/h; albumin 5% 500 mL over 4 hours starts at 0600 per the burn protocol.
The capillary leak and losses continue for 24 to 48 hours, so he still needs fluid; colloid (albumin) holds fluid in the vessels and lets you use less crystalloid.
Weight is up 7.6 kg, so the extra fluid is in the tissues (edema); also watch lung sounds and ventilator pressures, bladder pressure, the right arm compartments and urine output.

items.title: Alcohol and the Next Three Days
items.prompt: His ethanol level was 42 mg/dL at 0240 and he usually drinks 4 to 6 beers on weekends, more than that the night of the fire. (a) When could alcohol withdrawal begin, and when are seizures and delirium tremens most likely? (b) Why may you not see the signs yet? (c) Which two vitamins are ordered and why? (d) Name three signs you would watch for.
items.where: Lab Results (Toxicology); H&P (social history); MAR (thiamine and folic acid)

elements.t: Withdrawal can begin 6 to 24 hours after the last drink; seizures 12 to 48 hours; delirium tremens 48 to 96 hours, so counting from the last drink (about the time of the fire, Monday 0130) the highest risk for him is Wednesday to Friday.
Propofol, fentanyl and lorazepam are sedating and mask the signs; and he cannot talk.
Thiamine (prevents Wernicke encephalopathy, needed before or with glucose) and folic acid (deficiency in alcohol use).

Any three: tachycardia, hypertension, fever, tremor, sweating, agitation, hallucinations, seizure, difficulty sedating (needing more drug); use RASS and CAM-ICU because CIWA needs a patient who can talk.

items.title: The Agitation Event at 0245
items.prompt: Read the 0320 nursing note. Marcus (RASS -3 earlier) becomes restless, thrashes his head, bites the endotracheal tube and the ventilator pressure alarms sound. (a) In order, what do you check and do FIRST, before any medication, and why? (b) The provider orders lorazepam 1 mg IV. Name one concern about giving a benzodiazepine to this patient and one question you could ask the provider. (c) What are the rules for the soft wrist restraint you are using? (d) Besides rechecking RASS, CPOT and vital signs after the dose, what do you document and who do you notify?
items.where: Chart Review > Notes (Nursing Note 0320); Orders (soft wrist restraint, lorazepam); Flowsheets (RASS, CPOT, ventilator); MAR

elements.t: Stay with him and check for causes before sedating: airway/tube (depth 24 cm, cuff pressure, secretions, kinks, bite block), ventilator alarms and synchrony (call RT), oxygenation, pain (CPOT 1-2), full bladder or Foley problem, positioning, and withdrawal/delirium; keep him safe (no unplanned extubation). Give analgesia first if pain is possible.

Concern: benzodiazepines increase delirium, prolong ventilation and can mask withdrawal; the unit prefers analgesia-first and propofol/dexmedetomidine. A good question: can we increase the propofol or fentanyl instead, or is a one-time lorazepam dose acceptable while he is ventilated (reason: alcohol-withdrawal risk)? Lorazepam is high-alert: double check the dose.

Restraint rules (per the order and hospital policy): provider order that is renewed every calendar day, least restrictive method, check circulation and skin at least every 2 hours (the order says q2h; many policies also require release and range of motion), assess the continuing need, document, remove at extubation, family informed.

Document the event (time, behavior, cause search, response, RASS/CPOT before and after, lorazepam 1 mg IV at 0300 with the reason), notify Dr. Brandt (on-call intensivist, SBAR; done at 0255) and the charge nurse (B. Sutton), and update Jenna at the morning call.

items.title: Checking the Right Hand and the Abdomen
items.prompt: Compartment syndrome is a risk after a circumferential burn and a large fluid resuscitation. For each of the six Ps, write what you can or cannot check in Marcus (he is sedated and intubated) and what the chart showed at 2300-0300. Then name the abdominal check ordered every six hours.
items.where: Flowsheets > Musculoskeletal / Mobility (Right Hand Neurovascular check); Nursing Notes; Orders (bladder pressure)
cols: Can you check it in Marcus? How?

key.answer: Rows 1-6 worth 0.2 each (the P is named, a sensible way to check, and the chart finding); row 7 (bladder / intra-abdominal pressure) 0.3.

elements.t: Pain: out of proportion, with passive stretch; cannot be reported while sedated, so look for grimace/CPOT rise and a tense forearm. Chart: CPOT 1 (forearm soft).
Pallor (and cool temperature): fingers pink and warm. Chart: warm, cap refill 3 seconds.
Pulselessness: Doppler signals over the radial and ulnar arteries (cannot rely on palpation through edema). Chart: biphasic Doppler signals present.
Paresthesia: cannot be asked; sensation is not assessable while sedated. Chart: left hand not testable (sedated); right hand decreased in the burned area.
Paralysis: motion of the fingers, only when sedation is lightened (SAT at 0800). Chart: not testable yet.
Poikilothermia / tension: skin temperature compared with the left hand, and firmness of the forearm compartments. Chart: fingers warm; forearm compartments soft and compressible, swelling stable.
Bladder (intra-abdominal) pressure every 6 hours through the Foley: 12 mmHg at 2330; call the provider above 15 (abdominal compartment syndrome is above 20 with organ dysfunction).

items.title: Tube Feeding and Calories
items.prompt: Open the tube feeding order and the flowsheet. (a) Write the advancing schedule from 1000 Monday and the rate at 0600 on Tuesday. (b) The formula is Osmolite 1.5, which has 1.5 kcal per mL and 62.7 g of protein per liter: how many calories and grams of protein will he receive in 24 hours at 70 mL/h? (c) Give two reasons burn patients are fed early through the gut. (d) What do you check before advancing, and what do you do for a residual over 500 mL?
items.where: Orders (Osmolite 1.5); Flowsheets > GI (Diet / Feeding); Intake/Output; Chart Review (Nutrition Assessment)

elements.t: Start 20 mL/h at 1000, then increase 10 mL/h every 4 hours (30 at 1400, 40 at 1800, 50 at 2200, 60 at 0200) to the goal of 70 mL/h at 0600.
70 mL/h x 24 h = 1,680 mL; x 1.5 kcal/mL = 2,520 kcal; x 62.7 g/L = about 105 g protein (accept 100-110).

Any two: burns make the body hypermetabolic (needs about 2,400-2,500 kcal and extra protein); early feeding protects the gut lining and lowers bacterial translocation and infection; supports wound healing; reduces muscle loss and stress ulcers.

Check the position of the tube (OG at the mark), the residual, abdominal distention, bowel sounds, stool, glucose, and keep the head of the bed at 30 degrees; for a residual over 500 mL hold the feeding and call the provider (and do not hold feeds for dressing changes).

items.title: The Midnight and 0600 Labs
items.prompt: Open Lab Results and compare the 0000 and 0600 draws (and the 0500 albumin and coagulation labs) with the day shift values. Choose FOUR results. Write the values, why they happen in a burn patient on propofol and tube feeding, and what you do or ask for.
items.where: Lab Results (Chemistry, CBC, Coagulation, Blood Gas)
cols: What you do or ask for

key.answer: Any 4 rows of the bank; each row 0.375: values correct (0.125), reason (0.125), action (0.125).

elements.t: Phosphorus 3.0 (1200) -> 2.8 (1800) -> 2.4 (0000) -> 2.1 (0600) (low): burn losses, insulin and feeding drive phosphate into cells (refeeding), dilution. Report to the provider; replacement is usually ordered; low phosphorus weakens breathing muscles and the heart.
Magnesium 1.8 (1800) -> 1.7 -> 1.6 (low): dilution and losses; report for replacement (low magnesium makes low potassium hard to correct, so replace magnesium along with potassium).
Potassium 4.5 -> 3.9: the insulin infusion and feeds move potassium into cells; many protocols aim for 4.0 or higher; notify the provider and recheck with the next draw (K 5.0 at 1800).

Albumin 2.6 (low) and prealbumin 7.1 (low): plasma leak, dilution and the acute-phase response; they do not measure nutrition well in the first days of a burn, but explain the albumin 5% order and the dietitian follow-up.

Triglycerides 168 (high; baseline at about 48 h of propofol): propofol is a lipid emulsion (1.1 kcal/mL); report it, count the calories, and a level over about 400 means ask whether to change the sedative.
CK 1,120 -> 840 (falling): muscle injury is improving; keep adequate urine output.
Hemoglobin 12.4 and platelets 214: dilution; platelets still normal; watch for bleeding with heparin prophylaxis. WBC 15.2 is stress response, a baseline for later comparison.
Sodium 134 (low): lactated Ringer's has less sodium than the plasma and he is retaining fluid; watch; no correction needed now.

items.title: Propofol: Math and Safety
items.prompt: At 1900 on Monday the propofol is running at 35 mcg/kg/min. The bag is propofol 10 mg/mL and his weight is 82 kg. (a) Calculate the rate in mL/h. (b) Propofol gives 1.1 kcal per mL: how many calories does the sedation add in 24 hours? (c) Name two reasons you check the triglyceride level and two signs of propofol infusion syndrome. (d) Name two nursing actions for the bag and tubing.
items.where: MAR (propofol); Orders (propofol); Lab Results (Triglycerides); Flowsheets (RASS)

elements.t: 35 mcg/kg/min x 82 kg = 2,870 mcg/min x 60 = 172,200 mcg/h = 172.2 mg/h; at 10 mg/mL = 17.2 mL/h.
17.2 mL/h x 24 h = about 413 mL/day x 1.1 kcal = about 455 kcal/day (accept 450-460); count it as part of his calories.

Triglycerides: lipid load can raise them (his 168 is mildly high) and very high levels cause pancreatitis; check about every 2 to 3 days. Infusion syndrome: unexplained metabolic acidosis, rhabdomyolysis/rising CK, hyperkalemia, arrhythmia or heart failure, high triglycerides, kidney injury (any two).

Any two: aseptic technique and change the tubing and vial/bag every 12 hours (lipid grows bacteria), label, watch blood pressure with every rate increase, do not mix other drugs in the line, daily sedation interruption.

items.title: Handoff at 0650
items.prompt: It is 0650 on Tuesday. Write your SBAR handoff for J. Morales, RN, the day nurse. Use real numbers, include the events of the night, what is happening in the next few hours (look at the orders and MAR), and anything you would like the day team to follow up.
items.where: Everything you read and charted this night; Orders; MAR; Lab Results; Flowsheets

elements.t: Situation: patient/room, full code, burn 22% with inhalation injury, intubated; stable night: HR 96, BP 111/64, T 99.4, SpO2 98%, RASS -2 (goal -1 to -2 today), CPOT 1; urine output 37-47 mL/h (0.45-0.57 mL/kg/h).

Background: the first 24 hours of Parkland finished at 0130 (about 8,080 mL), LR 125 mL/h from 0130, then 75 mL/h since 0600 while albumin 5% runs; insulin infusion since 0030; feeds at goal 70 mL/h; weight 89.6 kg; the flowsheet shows the night shift (1900-0700) intake 3,748 mL, output 496 mL, net +3,252 mL.

Assessment: agitation at 0245 treated with lorazepam 1 mg (calm since); glucose 179-191 on the infusion (1.5 units/h since 0600); phosphorus 2.1 and magnesium 1.6 low and potassium down from 5.0 to 3.9, reported to Dr. Brandt, replacement planned after the noon labs and not given overnight; right hand signals steady; bladder pressure 12; triglycerides 168; skin and turns done.

Recommendation / to do: sedation interruption at 0800; noon labs and replace phosphorus, magnesium and potassium as ordered; hourly glucose; albumin 5% 500 mL running 0600-1000; dressing change and silver sulfadiazine at 1400 with hydromorphone beforehand; restraint order renewal; update Jenna and Linda; chest x-ray (0515: small new right lower lobe atelectasis, lines in place) so chest PT and turning; watch for alcohol withdrawal.

parts.title: Shift 3: Tuesday 11/03 0700 to 1900 (day shift)
parts.intro: Set the simulation clock to 0700 on Tuesday 11/03/26. You are J. Morales, RN, and you take report from the night nurse. Keep reading forward in the chart as the clock moves; do not look past 1900 for this shift. A quiet morning is followed by a change in condition in the afternoon.
parts.keyNote: Shift 3 follows the safe wake-up, the electrolyte orders, early recognition of burn wound infection (graph analysis, SBAR), the sepsis bundle with antibiotic checks, the norepinephrine math and the shock plan. A careful student should earn about 12 of the 16 points.

items.title: The 0800 Sedation Interruption
items.prompt: Set the clock to 0700 and read the 0850 nursing note and the 0845 respiratory therapy note. (a) What was done at 0800 and what was the order for the sedatives? (b) How did Marcus respond (RASS, commands, CAM-ICU, his mother)? (c) Name two findings that would make you stop the interruption early and restart the sedation. (d) Why is he NOT having a breathing trial (SBT) today even though FiO2 is 0.40 and PEEP is 5?
items.where: Chart Review > Notes (Nursing Note 0850, Respiratory Therapy Note 0845, ICU Progress Note 0715); Orders (SAT); MAR (propofol)

elements.t: Propofol held at 0800 (was 30 mcg/kg/min) while fentanyl 100 mcg/h continued for pain; the order says wake to RASS 0 to -1 or until agitation or distress, then restart at half the prior rate (restarted 0835 at 20 mcg/kg/min, back to 30 at 0930).

Woke to voice within minutes, RASS 0, followed commands with the LEFT hand and left leg, mouthed "mom", tearful, calmed holding his mother Linda's hand; CAM-ICU negative; HR 92-98, MAP 78-82, SpO2 98%, no dyssynchrony.

Any two stop criteria: agitation or distress, pulling at the tube or lines, ventilator dyssynchrony or biting, SpO2 under about 88-90%, sustained HR/BP change, respiratory rate over about 35, seizure or new arrhythmia, unsafe pain.

Still in the post-resuscitation fluid-shift phase (albumin 5% running until 1000, Parkland ended only at 0130), airway/facial edema, no cuff-leak test, a 1400 dressing change needing sedation and analgesia; reassess tomorrow (Dr. Brandt and RT).

items.title: Albumin and the Feeds
items.prompt: Albumin 5% 500 mL runs from 0600 to 1000. (a) Calculate the pump rate in mL/h. (b) Why is albumin given to Marcus now (use a lab value), and what two things do you assess during the infusion? (c) What did the LR rate change to at 1000? (d) The dietitian wrote about the tube feeding and the 1400 dressing change: what did she recommend about holding the feeding?
items.where: MAR (albumin 5%, lactated Ringer's); Lab Results (Albumin); Nursing Note 1030; Nutrition Follow-Up Note 1045; Flowsheets > Intake/Output

elements.t: Serum albumin 2.6 (low) and ongoing capillary leak: albumin holds fluid in the vessels, so less crystalloid is needed (he is already about 12% over the Parkland goal). Assess for fluid overload (lung sounds, SpO2, ventilator pressures, edema) and for reaction (fever, chills, hypotension, rash) plus urine output.
LR went from 75 mL/h to 100 mL/h at 1000 (titrate urine output 0.5-1 mL/kg/h).
Do NOT hold the feeding (Osmolite 1.5 at goal 70 mL/h) for dressing changes; hold only for the OR or extubation (and she added a protein modular 15 g twice a day).

items.title: Noon Electrolytes and the Replacement Orders
items.prompt: Open the 1200 labs, the orders and the MAR. For each result, write the value, the replacement ordered (drug, dose, route, rate) with the time you gave it, and the safety check or monitoring you do. Then answer below the table: why did the potassium and phosphorus drop when he is on an insulin infusion and tube feeding, and what other 1200 result could the phosphate make worse?
items.where: Lab Results (Chemistry, 1200); Orders; MAR (potassium chloride, magnesium sulfate, sodium phosphate); Nursing Note 1240

key.answer: Rows 0.4 each (value 0.1, order and time 0.15, safety 0.15) = 1.2; the two sentences below the table 0.3.

elements.t: Potassium 3.6 (goal 4.0 or higher): KCl 20 mEq in 100 mL over 2 h (10 mEq/h) through the central line, given 1230 and a second dose 1430. Safety: central line only, maximum 10 mEq/h, telemetry, separate pump, double check; hold and call for urine output under 30 mL/h for 2 hours; recheck K 4 h later.
Magnesium 1.7: magnesium sulfate 2 g in 50 mL over 1 h IV, given 1330. Safety: watch BP, HR and reflexes/respiration (hypotension, flushing); recheck level with the evening labs.

Phosphorus 2.1 (low): sodium phosphate 15 mmol in 250 mL over 4 h via the central line, started 1500. Safety: slow infusion, separate pump, watch calcium (7.6, low) and renal function; recheck with the evening labs.

Insulin and feeding (refeeding) drive K and phosphorus into the cells, plus burn and fluid losses and dilution. Phosphate binds calcium and can lower an already low calcium (Ca 7.6): watch for tingling, cramps, QT change and ask about the calcium.

items.title: The 1400 Dressing Change
items.prompt: You and N. Ibarra, RN (burn nurse specialist) change the dressings. Read the 1425 and 1455 notes. (a) List the four NEW findings that told you this is not a normal burn wound. (b) What pain medicine was given, when, and how did CPOT change? (c) What did you do to the edge of the red area at 1430 and why? (d) Which finding at the right chest border is the most worrisome for tissue death?
items.where: Chart Review > Notes (Nursing Note 1425, Wound Care Specialist Note 1455); MAR (hydromorphone); Flowsheets (CPOT)

elements.t: New since Monday: purulent drainage (thick yellow-green) on the chest/arm dressings; foul odor; erythema spreading beyond the burn margin (about 2-3 cm in the notes, 4 cm on the 1430 flowsheet entry; warm, indurated); eschar separating with a dark violaceous area. (Any four of these, including increased pain with cleansing.)
Hydromorphone 0.5 mg IV at 1345, 15 minutes before the change; CPOT 2/8 at 1300, 5/8 during dressing removal, back to 4 by 1500.
Marked the margin of erythema with a skin marker (dated and timed 1430), measured and photographed, to see whether it spreads; recheck every 4 hours and every shift.
The dark violaceous, non-blanching area about 4 x 5 cm at the right chest border with loss of eschar adherence: possible invasive infection with tissue necrosis (needs surgeon exam and biopsy).

items.title: Analyze the Graph: Temperature, Heart Rate and MAP
items.prompt: Study the figure (it is drawn from the flowsheet for 0700 to 1900). (a) At about what time did the change begin and which of the three values moved first? (b) Describe the pattern at 1400, 1700 and 1900 in your own words and say what it means for Marcus. (c) After the norepinephrine starts at 1730 the MAP climbs back up: what does the graph tell you about whether he is getting better? (d) Burn patients often have a fast heart rate and a temperature near 100 F even when they are well: why are the usual SIRS criteria unreliable for him, and name two signs you use instead.
items.where: Flowsheets > Vital Signs (Tuesday 0700-1900); Notes (Critical Care Event Note 1755); the figure below

images.caption: Figure: Marcus Delaney, temperature, heart rate and MAP, Tuesday 0700 to 1900.

elements.t: Stable all morning (T 99.4-99.7, HR 92-98, MAP 77-80); the change starts about 1300 (T 99.9, a slow creep from 1100), and the sharp bend is between 1300 and 1400. Temperature moved first (slowly, from 99.7 to 99.9); then HR (97 to 105) and MAP (77 to 72) changed together at 1400.

Steady rise of temperature (100.4 at 1400, 101.6 at 1700, 102.3 at 1900) and HR (105, 122, 130) with falling MAP (72, 66, then 63 at 1715, below the goal of 65): the picture of evolving sepsis from the wound infection, going into septic shock (vasodilation and low perfusion); it is a trend, not a single value.

MAP recovers (64 to 70) because the drug squeezes the vessels, but temperature and heart rate keep climbing (HR 130, T 102.3), so the infection is not controlled; he is not better, the pressor treats the number, not the cause (needs source control: antibiotics, surgery, fluids carefully).

He is already hypermetabolic after the burn (baseline HR above 90 and temperature 99-100 F, tachypnea, high WBC and glucose), so SIRS criteria are met by almost every burn patient and do not separate sepsis. Better: trend (progressive tachycardia over 110, temperature over about 102 F/39 C, RR over 25), new hyperglycemia/insulin resistance (glucose 205-244), falling platelets, feeding intolerance, falling urine output, rising lactate, wound changes. (Accept any two.)

items.title: The SBAR Call at 1540
items.prompt: It is 1540. You are going to call Dr. Okafor and Dr. Brandt. Write what you say (S, B, A, R) using the chart numbers at 1530 and the trend since 1300. End with what you ask them for: name at least three orders or decisions you request.
items.where: Flowsheets > Vital Signs, Intake/Output, Lab Results; Notes (Nursing Note 1550 Sepsis SBAR)

elements.t: Situation: bed/name, suspected burn wound infection with sepsis; 1530 T 101.1 F, HR 113, BP 105/51 (MAP 69), RR 23, SpO2 96% on the ventilator.

Background: 34-year-old man, 22% TBSA flame burn with inhalation injury, post-burn day 2, intubated, NKDA, full code; 1400 dressing change findings (purulent drainage, foul odor, spreading erythema, violaceous eschar at the right chest border).

Assessment: trend T 99.9 (1300), 100.4, 100.9, 101.1; HR 97, 105, 108, 113; MAP 77, 72, 71, 69; RR 18 to 23; urine 45, 41, 36 mL/h (0.44 mL/kg/h, falling); glucose 205 at 1530 (was 173); WBC 15.4 and lactate 1.4 earlier; CPOT 4. "I am concerned this is early sepsis."

Recommendation: bedside wound exam by the surgeon; sepsis order set: cultures before antibiotics (blood x2, wound, tracheal aspirate, urine), lactate, procalcitonin, CBC with differential, coags; broad-spectrum antibiotics after cultures; fluids or MAP plan; call parameters (MAP under 65, urine under 30 mL/h). (Any three requests.)

items.title: The Sepsis Bundle: Cultures and Lactate
items.prompt: Open the 1655 nursing note and Lab Results. (a) List the four culture sites (five specimens) and the time collected, and which two blood sites. (b) Why must the cultures be drawn BEFORE the antibiotics, and when is it OK to give antibiotics without waiting? (c) Write the lactate values and times from 1555 to 1700 and what they mean. (d) What is the goal for giving antibiotics after recognizing sepsis, and what were Marcus's actual times?
items.where: Chart Review > Notes (Nursing Note 1655, Burn Surgery Event Note 1645); Lab Results (Microbiology, Lactate, Procalcitonin); MAR

elements.t: Collected 1550: blood culture set 1 peripheral (left hand), set 2 from the left IJ central line, wound swab (right chest/arm, after cleansing, from the drainage), tracheal aspirate, urine from the Foley port; all labeled and sent. (Wound biopsy 1635 by Dr. Okafor.)

Antibiotics kill or suppress the organisms and a culture drawn afterward can be falsely negative, so you could not target or narrow therapy; draw before the first dose, but in septic shock the antibiotics must not be delayed (goal within 1 hour); if cultures cannot be obtained quickly, give the antibiotics and document why.

Lactate 2.9 at 1555 (high), 3.8 at 1700 (rising): tissue hypoperfusion (anaerobic metabolism); the rise despite maintenance fluids (the first bolus did not start until 1700) means he is getting worse, repeat in 2 hours (goal clearance 10-20% every 2 hours). Also WBC 18.4, procalcitonin 4.8 at 1555.
Antibiotics within 1 hour of recognition: recognized and SBAR 1540, cultures 1550, pip-tazo 1630 (about 50 minutes after the call), vancomycin 1645 (about 65 minutes).

items.title: Checking the Antibiotic Orders
items.prompt: Before you hang the antibiotics you check the orders with pharmacy (A. Chen, PharmD). Marcus weighs 82 kg. (a) The vancomycin load is 20 mg/kg: calculate the dose and compare it with the 1,750 mg on the MAR, then give the pump rate in mg/h for the 2-hour infusion and the order's maximum rate. (b) The piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g in 100 mL is an extended infusion: over how long, at what mL/h, and why is it given this way? (c) What does the pip-tazo order say about running it with the vancomycin, and what will you do with the lumens of the left IJ? (d) Name two lab values you follow with this combination and why.
items.where: Orders (piperacillin-tazobactam, vancomycin); MAR; Lab Results (Creatinine); Nursing Note 1655

elements.t: 20 mg/kg x 82 kg = 1,640 mg; the 1,750 mg is 21.3 mg/kg, about 7% above 1,640 mg (the order says "about 20 mg/kg, rounded to 1,750 mg", the nearest 250 mg; pharmacy verified). 1,750 mg / 2 h = 875 mg/h, under the order maximum of 1 g/h (slow the rate if red man syndrome).
Infuse over 4 hours: 100 mL / 4 h = 25 mL/h. Extended infusion keeps the drug level above the organism MIC for longer (time-dependent beta-lactam), which helps in sepsis and with Pseudomonas.

The order says to give pip-tazo through its own lumen when possible, separate from vancomycin, and that the combination is associated with kidney injury (pharmacy also advises no co-infusion because compatibility depends on the concentration); run them on separate lumens/pumps of the left IJ (the norepinephrine later gets its own lumen too, never shared), and ask pharmacy if lumens run short.

Creatinine (1.1 at 1700; vancomycin and pip-tazo are nephrotoxic, and his urine output is falling) and vancomycin levels (pharmacy AUC dosing); also watch WBC/temperature for response and check the cultures to narrow in 48 hours.

items.title: Low MAP and Norepinephrine
items.prompt: At 1715 the BP is 101/44 (MAP 63-64) after the 1700 LR bolus; the second bolus is given at 1745 and norepinephrine 16 mcg/mL is started at 1730 at 0.05 mcg/kg/min. (a) Calculate the pump rate in mL/h for 0.05 mcg/kg/min (82 kg), and the rate at 0.10 mcg/kg/min that you reached at 1830. (b) Where must it run and why (name the complication and one sign)? (c) How and how fast do you titrate, and what is the MAP goal and how is the MAP measured? (d) Why do the providers want to limit more fluid boluses?
items.where: Orders (norepinephrine, LR bolus); MAR; Nursing Note 1755; Critical Care Event Note 1755; Flowsheets > Vital Signs

elements.t: 0.05 x 82 = 4.1 mcg/min x 60 = 246 mcg/h / 16 mcg/mL = 15.4 mL/h. At 0.10: 8.2 mcg/min = 492 mcg/h = 30.8 mL/h (as printed on the order).

Central line only, on a dedicated lumen with nothing else in it (never a PIV): extravasation causes tissue necrosis; check the site and the hand/extremity every hour (pain, blanching, swelling, cool skin, loss of blood return); if suspected stop the drip and notify the provider at once (the provider may order phentolamine; follow the unit extravasation protocol).

Titrate by 0.02 mcg/kg/min every 5 minutes (order; max 0.5 without attending approval) to MAP 65 or higher; wean by 0.02 every 15-30 minutes when MAP is over 75; MAP read from the left radial arterial line (leveled and zeroed); give a second RN check for each change; she went 0.05, 0.08 (1800), 0.10 (1830).

He is already about 12% over the Parkland total with moderate edema, the rising airway pressures (PIP 24 to 28, Pplat 17 to 21) and SpO2 falling from 98% to 95% suggest leak into the lungs, and the boluses lifted MAP only briefly; more fluid worsens edema and ARDS risk. Give vasopressor instead.

items.title: Switching the Topical Antimicrobial
items.prompt: Silver sulfadiazine was stopped and mafenide acetate 5% soaks were started at 1730. (a) Why did the burn surgeon choose mafenide for this wound? (b) Name the two things you monitor with mafenide and look at the 1700 bicarbonate and the 1845 arterial blood gas: what do they show and why can you not blame the mafenide alone? (c) What do you give before each soak and how often are they done?
items.where: Orders (mafenide, silver sulfadiazine); MAR; Lab Results (Chemistry 1700, Blood Gas 1845, Lactate); Burn Surgery Event Note 1645

elements.t: Mafenide penetrates eschar and wound tissue (the infection is under separating eschar), unlike silver sulfadiazine which does not; it is active against the Gram-negatives and many organisms in the wound.

Monitor metabolic acidosis (mafenide is a carbonic anhydrase inhibitor: BMP/bicarbonate and ABG) and pain/burning on application. Chart: CO2 23 (1200) to 22 (1700); ABG 1845 pH 7.31, HCO3 18, base excess -8, PaCO2 36. This is a real metabolic acidosis, but lactate was already 3.8 at 1700 (septic shock) so the cause is mainly lactic acidosis, and mafenide can add to it: report it and trend.
Pain medicine (hydromorphone/fentanyl) before the soak; soaks every 8 hours (next 0130), keep the gauze moist.

items.title: Falling Urine Output
items.prompt: The urine output was 45, 41, 36, 28, 24 and 20 mL per hour from 1200 to 1800 (his goal is 0.5 mL/kg/h = 41 mL/h, and Foley care is done). At 1800 the output is 20 mL (0.24 mL/kg/h). Which actions are correct for you now?
items.where: Flowsheets > Intake/Output and Vital Signs; Nursing Note 1240 (potassium plan); MAR; Lab Results (Creatinine); Notes 1755
options: Report it to Dr. Brandt and Dr. Okafor now (it is below the 30 mL/h call limit) and tie it to the MAP and lactate.
Check the Foley for kinks, a full bag tubing loop or sediment, and the bladder pressure (last 12 mmHg).
Ask the provider whether to give a third 500 mL LR bolus because he is oliguric, without looking at his lungs or total fluid balance.
Hold any further potassium replacement and tell the provider (your 1240 plan was to hold potassium for urine output under 30 mL/h for 2 hours; it has been under 30 since 1500).
Ask about the doses of nephrotoxic drugs (vancomycin, pip-tazo) with pharmacy and follow the creatinine.
Stop the norepinephrine to see if the urine improves.
Keep recording hourly urine output and total I&O; remember he is also getting feeds and fluids, so urine output is the better marker.
Give furosemide to make urine because the output is low.

answer: Report it to Dr. Brandt and Dr. Okafor now...
Hold any further potassium replacement and tell the provider...
Ask about the doses of nephrotoxic drugs...
Keep recording hourly urine output and total I&O...
key.rules: About 0.2 per correct option selected (5 correct = 1.0); subtract 0.2 for each wrong option selected (not below 0). Wrong: asking for another bolus without assessing (he is 12% over Parkland, edema, new lung findings and rising pressures; the oliguria is from low perfusion/sepsis), stopping the norepinephrine (MAP 63-64 would fall), a diuretic in septic shock (would worsen perfusion and kidney injury). By 1900 the chart totals for the shift are 4,094 in, 474 out, +3,620 net.
key.errors: Treating the number (more fluid or a diuretic) without looking for the cause, or not reporting it.

items.title: Handoff at 1850
items.prompt: It is 1850. Write your SBAR handoff for E. Haddad, RN, the night nurse. Use real numbers from your shift, say what is changing, and list what the night nurse must do or follow up in the next hours (look at the orders, MAR and labs).
items.where: Everything charted this shift; Orders; MAR; Lab Results; Flowsheets (Vital Signs, Intake/Output); Nursing Note 1850

elements.t: Situation: septic shock from a right chest/arm burn wound infection; 1830 T 102.1 F, HR 126, BP 108/48 (MAP 68), RR 29, SpO2 94%; on norepinephrine 0.10 mcg/kg/min (30.8 mL/h) to keep MAP 65 or higher; full code, NKDA.

Background: 22% TBSA flame burn with inhalation injury, post-burn day 2, intubated; Parkland ended 0130; wound infection found at 1400; cultures x4 sites 1550; pip-tazo 1630 (extended, 4 h) and vancomycin 1,750 mg 1645 (until about 1845) on separate lumens; LR 500 mL x2 (1700, 1745); norepinephrine started 1730 (0.05, 0.08 at 1800, 0.10 at 1830); mafenide started 1730, silver sulfadiazine stopped; biopsy 1635.

Assessment: lactate 2.9 then 3.8 (repeat due 1900); ABG 1845 pH 7.31, HCO3 18, BE -8; urine 20 mL/h (0.24 mL/kg/h); glucose 244 on insulin 4 units/h (feeds still 70 mL/h); ventilator changed at 1800 to PEEP 8, FiO2 0.50, rate 18, PIP 29/Pplat 22 (early ARDS physiology, portable chest x-ray); propofol 40, fentanyl 150, RASS -3; WBC 18.4, procalcitonin 4.8, platelets 171, INR 1.4. Day shift I&O (EHR): 4,094 in, 474 out, +3,620 net.

Recommendation: titrate norepinephrine for MAP 65 or higher and call Dr. Brandt if the dose keeps rising (vasopressin above 0.25, hydrocortisone considered); lactate at 1900 and ABG; hourly glucose and urine output (call for under 20 mL/h); follow cultures and biopsy; mafenide soaks every 8 hours (next 0130) with pain premedication and acid-base watch; re-mark the erythema margin every 4 hours; hourly right-hand neurovascular checks; recheck K, Mg and phosphorus; central line and extravasation checks; family at the bedside.

parts.title: Shift 4: Tuesday 11/03 1900 to Wednesday 11/04 0700 (night shift)
parts.step: The peak of the burn wound sepsis
parts.intro: Set the simulation clock to 1900 on Tuesday 11/03/26. You take report from J. Morales, RN, and care for Marcus (burn wound septic shock on norepinephrine) until you hand off at 0700. Keep reading forward in the chart as the clock moves; do not look past 0700 for this shift.
parts.keyNote: Shift 4 is the sepsis peak and recovery: shock recognition, vasopressor math and weaning (graph), steroids and insulin, a critical culture call, and AKI with two nephrotoxic antibiotics. Watch for the traps: HIT is not the answer to the platelet fall, the 0200 output of 280 mL is mostly stool, and the pressor is never turned down in a hypothetical falling MAP. A careful student should earn about 12 of the 16 points.

items.title: The Peak of the Sepsis
items.where: Flowsheets > Vital Signs; Chart Review > Notes (Nursing Note 1950)
items.prompt: Set the clock to 1930 on Tuesday. Copy the vital signs at each time, circle every abnormal value, then answer below: (a) Calculate the mean arterial pressure at 1930 from the blood pressure and compare it with the MAP on the monitor. (b) Why is a MAP of about 69 NOT reassuring in Marcus at 1930?

key.rules: Cells 0.75 x (cells correct / 20), rounded to the nearest 0.25; the two answers are 0.25 together (0.125 each). Allow +/- 2 for rates and +/- 0.2 F. Values: 1930: T 102.4, HR 133, BP 107/50, RR 30, SpO2 92; 2300: T 101.4, HR 117, BP 111/55, RR 26, SpO2 96; 0300: T 100.5, HR 108, BP 111/60, RR 20, SpO2 98; 0600: T 100.2, HR 101, BP 110/59, RR 19, SpO2 97. (a) MAP = (107 + 2 x 50) / 3 = 69 mmHg, which matches the monitor (69). (b) The MAP of 69 is only being kept above the goal of 65 by norepinephrine (0.10 at 1900, 0.12 at 1930, 0.14 from 2030), with fever 102.4, HR 133, RR 30 and lactate 4.1: he is in septic shock and the pressure would fall without the drug. The diastolic of 50 shows vasodilation.

items.title: MAP calculation and why 69 is not reassuring (scored with 4.1)
The 1845 Blood Gas
items.prompt: Open Lab Results (Blood Gas) and the ventilator settings for 1845. (a) Interpret the ABG in one sentence (acid-base disorder and what the body is doing about it) and name the lab drawn at 1900 that explains it. (b) Calculate the PaO2/FiO2 ratio and say what the chest x-ray at 1840 adds.
items.where: Lab Results (Blood Gas, Lactate); Chart Review > Notes (Dr. Brandt 1755, Nursing Note 1850 for the ventilator change); Chart Review > Imaging (Chest X-Ray 1840)

elements.t: pH 7.31, HCO3 18, base excess -8 = metabolic acidosis (PaCO2 36 is low-normal because he is breathing at 30 per minute: respiratory compensation, not a respiratory problem). Explained by the lactate of 4.1 at 1900 (lactic acidosis from shock); mafenide soaks can also add to a metabolic acidosis.

PaO2 92 / FiO2 0.50 = 184 (accept 180-190): a P/F under 200 on PEEP 8 is in the moderate ARDS range; the x-ray shows new bilateral perihilar/interstitial opacities, no consolidation = early ARDS physiology (capillary leak of sepsis), which is why the vent was changed to PEEP 8 and FiO2 0.50 at 1800 (set RR 18).

items.title: Norepinephrine: Rate and Safety
items.prompt: Open the MAR and the Orders. Norepinephrine 16 mcg/mL was 0.10 mcg/kg/min at 1900, 0.12 at 1930 and 0.14 at 2030. His dosing weight is 82 kg. (a) Calculate the pump rate in mL/h at 0.14 mcg/kg/min. (b) What MAP are you titrating to, and why is the arterial line and a central lumen used? (c) Give two safety checks for a vasopressor infusion.
items.where: MAR (norepinephrine); Orders; Chart Review > Notes (Nursing Note 1755, Dr. Brandt 1755)

elements.t: 0.14 mcg/kg/min x 82 kg = 11.48 mcg/min x 60 = 688.8 mcg/h; / 16 mcg/mL = 43 mL/h (accept 43.0-43.1).

MAP 65 mmHg or higher (order: titrate by 0.02 mcg/kg/min every 5 minutes; the notes allow 0.02-0.04 every 5-10 minutes; accept either). A-line gives beat-to-beat pressure while the dose is changing; vasopressors are given through a central, dedicated lumen because they cause severe vasoconstriction and tissue injury if they leak into the skin.

Any two: independent double check of the concentration and rate; do not flush or bolus the line; hourly site check of the left IJ (swelling, blanching) and stop/notify per protocol if infiltration is suspected; level and zero the transducer; never stop it abruptly; keep a back-up ready; titrate only per the order.

items.title: Hydrocortisone, Glucose and the Insulin Infusion
items.prompt: Open the MAR, the Orders, Lab Results (point-of-care glucose and potassium) and the pharmacy note of 1930. (a) Hydrocortisone 50 mg IV q6h started at 2030: why would Dr. Brandt order a stress dose, and how many doses did you give this shift? (b) List the glucose values at 1930, 2130 and 0230 and the insulin rate changes between 1900 and 0300, and explain why the glucose rose after the steroid. (c) Why were the insulin rates lowered, and what is the hypoglycemia risk in Marcus? (d) Which electrolyte do you watch with insulin, and what were his values?
items.where: MAR (hydrocortisone, insulin infusion); Lab Results (Glucose, Potassium); Chart Review > Notes (Pharmacy 1930, Dr. Brandt 2345)

elements.t: Septic shock that still needs norepinephrine at 0.1 or higher (0.14 at 2030): critical illness can cause a relative adrenal insufficiency; hydrocortisone helps the vessels respond to norepinephrine and shortens time on the pressor. Two doses given by the night nurse: 2030 and 0230 (next 0830); the order is 50 mg q6h for 3 doses (third due 0830), then 25 mg q6h until the ICU team stops it; pharmacy plans a taper once off pressors, so never stop it abruptly.

Glucose 246 (1930), 251 (2030), 266 (2130, peak), then 257, 241, 225, 212, 197 (0230). Insulin 4 units/h (running since 1800), raised to 5 at 2100, 3 at 0000, 1.5 at 0300. Hydrocortisone (a glucocorticoid) and sepsis stress hormones cause insulin resistance and more glucose release from the liver; the glucose was already rising with the sepsis (227 at 1730) and the peak came about one hour after the first dose.

Rates are lowered as the glucose falls toward the goal 140-180 mg/dL and as the sepsis improves (less insulin resistance). Risk of hypoglycemia: insulin requirement falls quickly while the feeding is constant at 70 mL/h; if the tube feeding is held or stops (OR, residual, tube problem) the glucose can drop fast; check hourly and after every rate change; per the order: glucose under 100 or tube feeding held = hold the infusion and call the provider; glucose under 70 = notify and give D50 per protocol, recheck.
Potassium: insulin moves potassium into the cells (hypokalemia). K 3.8 (1700), 4.0 (2300), 4.1 (0500): acceptable, but keep 4.0 or higher, replace per protocol, and check with each BMP.

items.title: The 2100 Labs and the 2130 Gram Stain
items.prompt: Open the CBC at 2100 (compare with 1555 and with admission) and the wound Gram stain at 2130. (a) What do a WBC of 21.8 with 14% bands tell you? (b) Platelets fell from 171 to 142 (and were 288 on admission) while he receives heparin 5,000 units SQ: what percent fall from admission is that, and what do you ask or check before you decide to hold the heparin? (c) What does "Gram-positive cocci in clusters" most likely mean, and do the antibiotics already cover it? (d) What does contact precautions mean for you today?
items.where: Lab Results (CBC with differential, Microbiology); Chart Review > Notes (Result Notification 2140); Orders (Precautions)

elements.t: WBC 21.8 (up from 18.4) with 14% bands (immature neutrophils, a "left shift") = the bone marrow is being driven hard by a serious bacterial infection; consistent with burn wound sepsis (segs 68%).

(288 - 142) / 288 = 51% fall since admission (already 128 at 0500 = 56%). Pharmacy asks to assess for HIT when platelets fall more than 50%: do not simply hold or continue; report the number and ask the provider; Dr. Brandt judged HIT unlikely (timing under 5 days of heparin, sepsis explains it). Watch for bleeding, trend platelets with the next CBC, and look at INR/fibrinogen for DIC (INR 1.3, fibrinogen 350 at 0500).

Gram-positive cocci in clusters = Staphylococcus, most likely S. aureus (suspected MSSA; MRSA not excluded until the culture finishes); a Gram stain is preliminary and does not give the antibiotic susceptibility. Vancomycin plus pip-tazo already cover it, so no change was ordered; wait for the final culture and sensitivities. The lab called the result at 2130 and the nurse called Dr. Brandt with read-back; Dr. Okafor to be told.

Contact precautions (burn unit): single room, gown and gloves for room entry and all wound care (plus mask for dressing changes), dedicated equipment (stethoscope, cuff), hand hygiene before and after, clean/dirty zones, sign on the door; accept equivalent items (the order says gown and gloves for all wound care and room entry, dedicated equipment). S. aureus spreads by hands and equipment.

items.title: Fever and Cooling
items.prompt: Open the temperature trend and the MAR (acetaminophen) from 1900 to 0600. (a) Write the temperature at 1930, 2200, 0000, 0300 and 0600 and the times acetaminophen 1 g IV was given. (b) Why record the temperature before you give acetaminophen, and why can you not give all the credit for the falling fever to acetaminophen? (c) Name two cooling measures you used or could use in a burn patient, and one thing you avoid.
items.where: Flowsheets > Vital Signs (Temperature, bladder); MAR (acetaminophen); Chart Review > Notes (Nursing Note 1950); Lab Results (AST, ALT)

elements.t: Acetaminophen lowers the temperature and can mask the true fever curve; record the temperature before the dose so the team sees the real trend. The fever was already falling before the 2200 dose (102.4 at 1930 -> 101.9 at 2100) and kept falling as the antibiotics, steroids and source control worked, so the fall is partly acetaminophen and partly a real response. (AST 96/ALT 84 at 0500: keep to 3 g/day.)

Any two: remove extra linens, lower room temperature, cool cloths to axillae/groin away from burns, fan; core temperature monitoring (bladder probe every 30 minutes). Avoid: ice baths or cold water on the burn wounds (heat loss and hypothermia) and shivering, which raises oxygen use and heart rate.

items.title: Mafenide Soaks
items.prompt: The right arm and chest are treated with mafenide 5% soaks every 8 hours (1730, 0130). (a) Why is the pain different with this agent, and how do you score it in Marcus? (b) Mafenide can cause an acid-base problem: which one, and which lab results from this night would you check?
items.where: MAR (mafenide, hydromorphone); Orders; Flowsheets (CPOT); Lab Results (Blood Gas, BMP)

elements.t: Mafenide penetrates eschar but causes burning pain on application; premedicate with the ordered analgesic 15 minutes before the soak (order: hydromorphone 15 minutes before dressing changes; the MAR shows 0.5 mg at 1915 for wound care discomfort, and none is charted before the 0130 soak, so a good answer notes the 0130 soak should be premedicated) and score pain with the CPOT because he is intubated and cannot report pain (CPOT 1/8 hourly after 1930).

It inhibits carbonic anhydrase and can cause a metabolic acidosis (hyperchloremic): check ABG pH/HCO3 and the BMP bicarbonate and chloride (HCO3 18 at 1845, 20 at 2230, 22 at 0400; CO2 22, 21, 22 and chloride 107, 106, 106 on the BMPs, so no worsening acidosis); report a falling bicarbonate or rising chloride.

items.title: Sedation and Delirium Risk
items.prompt: Open the Orders (RASS goal), the flowsheet and the MAR. (a) What is the RASS goal for Tuesday, what was his RASS (charted 2000, 0000 and 0400) on propofol 40 mcg/kg/min and fentanyl 150 mcg/h, and why did Dr. Brandt accept the deeper sedation tonight? (b) Name two delirium risk factors he has and two things you do about them.
items.where: Orders (Sedation and pain scales); Flowsheets (RASS, CAM-ICU, Respiratory); MAR (propofol, fentanyl); Chart Review > Notes (Dr. Brandt 2345)

elements.t: Goal -1 to -2 on Tuesday; his RASS was -3 at 2000 and 0000 (deeper than the goal) because he was triggering the ventilator (RR 30) in septic shock with early ARDS (PEEP 8, FiO2 0.50) and needed comfort and synchrony; no SAT tonight (Dr. Brandt). When he improved, propofol was lowered to 30 and fentanyl to 100 at 0400 and RASS became -2.

Any two risks: sepsis, deep sedation/fentanyl, mechanical ventilation, steroids, sleep loss, restraint, alcohol use (withdrawal window 48-96 h is Wed-Thu); actions: CAM-ICU every shift (negative at 2000, 0000, 0400), lowest effective sedation and analgesia first, lights/noise down at night, cluster care, reorient and talk to him, family at the bedside, avoid benzodiazepines, remove restraints when not needed.

items.title: Septic Shock That Is Not Responding
items.stem: HYPOTHETICAL (not in the chart): at 2100 the monitor shows MAP 58 mmHg, HR 134 and urine output 12 mL/h for 2 hours while the norepinephrine is running at 0.14 mcg/kg/min through the left IJ central line. Which nursing actions are appropriate for Marcus?
items.prompt: Choose all that apply.
items.where: Think through the sepsis bundle, MAR (norepinephrine, hydrocortisone) and Orders; this scenario is not in the chart.
options: Notify Dr. Brandt now with SBAR: MAP under 65 on a rising dose of norepinephrine.
Check the arterial line (level, zero, compare with a cuff pressure) and confirm the pump rate, concentration and lumen.
Turn the norepinephrine down for a few minutes to see whether his pressure recovers on its own.
Move the norepinephrine to the left antecubital peripheral IV so the central line can be used for fluid.
Expect orders for a second vasopressor (for example vasopressin) and give any ordered fluid in measured boluses, listening to the lungs and watching the ventilator pressures after each one.
Give lactated Ringer's wide open until the MAP is above 65, because burn patients always need more fluid.
Hold the next hydrocortisone and antibiotic doses until the blood pressure improves.
Look for other causes of a falling pressure: bleeding, a tense abdomen (bladder pressure over 15 mmHg), a pneumothorax on the ventilator and the effect of propofol and fentanyl.
Recheck the lactate and glucose, keep hourly urine output and neurovascular checks, and document the times and the notifications.

answer: Notify Dr. Brandt now with SBAR...
Check the arterial line (level, zero, compare with a cuff pressure)...
Expect orders for a second vasopressor... measured boluses...
Look for other causes of a falling pressure...
Recheck the lactate and glucose, keep hourly urine output...
key.rules: 0.2 per correct option selected; subtract 0.2 for each incorrect option selected (not below 0). Wrong options: turning the pressor down (it is the treatment, never reduce or stop it without an order); a peripheral IV for the main vasopressor (central lumen is the standard; only short term with protocol); unlimited fluid (burn patients and the early ARDS lungs, PEEP 8, edema 2-3+ and weight gain make fluid creep dangerous); holding the steroid and antibiotics (both are part of the shock treatment and are given on time).

items.title: The Critical Result at 0240
items.prompt: Open Lab Results (Microbiology) and the nursing note of 0300. At 0240 the microbiology lab calls you. (a) What do you do during the call (what do you say and write down)? (b) Who do you notify, and in what time frame? (c) Write the SBAR you give with the real values. (d) Which line is involved, and what do you assess at the bedside?
items.where: Lab Results (Blood culture 0240); Chart Review > Notes (Critical Result Call 0300, Pharmacy 1930); Flowsheets; Orders (central line care)

elements.t: Write the result down (or enter it) with the caller's name and the time, read it back (patient name and second identifier, blood culture set 2 from the central line, bottle 1 of 4 positive at 10 hours, Gram-positive cocci in clusters) and get the caller to verify it ("read back verified"); document the time of the call (0240).

Dr. Brandt (intensivist) was called at 0245; also tell the charge nurse and make sure Dr. Okafor (burn surgeon) and pharmacy (A. Chen) are aware; critical results go to a provider immediately (within the policy time, usually 15-30 minutes at most) and the response and any order are documented.

S: critical blood culture, 1 of 4 bottles, central line set, GPC in clusters. B: burn wound sepsis, cultures drawn 1550 before antibiotics, vancomycin and pip-tazo since the evening, wound Gram stain also GPC in clusters at 2130, left IJ line day 3. A: about 0200-0300 T 100.5-100.7, HR 107-108, BP 109-111/55-60 (MAP 73-77), lactate 1.8 (0200), norepinephrine 0.08, improving; line site clean. R: ask whether to continue vancomycin and pip-tazo (next vancomycin 0430), when to repeat blood cultures, and who decides about the line once the organism is identified (ID consult).

Left IJ triple lumen (placed Monday 0345): dressing dry, intact and dated; look and feel for erythema, drainage, tenderness and neck swelling; flush each lumen and check blood return; hub scrub 15 seconds; review whether it is still needed (norepinephrine and antibiotics): it stays until the team decides; do not remove it on your own. One positive bottle can be a contaminant, but with a matching wound Gram stain and S. aureus likely, treat it as real until the identification returns.

items.title: Reading the Pressor Graph
items.prompt: Study the graph of MAP, norepinephrine dose and lactate for this shift. (a) What happened to the MAP while the dose was raised from 0.10 to 0.14 and then lowered to zero? (b) How did the lactate change, and what does that mean? (c) What did you need to see before it was safe to wean, and who sets the criteria? (d) After the pressor is off, what do you watch, and what would make you call the provider?
items.where: Flowsheets > Vital Signs (MAP); MAR (norepinephrine); Lab Results (Lactate); Chart Review > Notes (Dr. Brandt 2345, Nursing Note 0450)

images.caption: Figure: MAP, norepinephrine dose and lactate, Tuesday 1900 to Wednesday 0700.

elements.t: From 1900 to about 2130 the MAP stayed flat at 69-71 even though the dose was raised 0.10 -> 0.12 (1930) -> 0.14 (2030): more drug was needed just to hold above 65 (worst of the sepsis). By 2300-0000 the MAP climbed to 73-75 on the same 0.14 (antibiotics, steroid and albumin working). From 0000 the dose was stepped down (0.12, 0.08 at 0200, 0.04 at 0400, off 0430) and the MAP stayed 73-78, never below 65: no fall off the pressor.

Lactate 4.1 (1900) -> 2.6 (2230) -> 1.8 (0200) -> 1.5 (0500): a fall of about 37% in 3.5 hours ((4.1 - 2.6) / 4.1), normal (under 2) by 0200. A falling lactate means the tissues are getting enough blood flow and oxygen (less anaerobic metabolism); a rising lactate would mean worse shock.

MAP at or above goal (65, here 73-77) on a stable, low dose; lactate falling or normal; urine output at least 0.5 mL/kg/h (41 mL/h for 82 kg; he made 51-68 mL/h); warm skin, brisk capillary refill, heart rate coming down (133 to 108), no new fluid bolus, infection treated. The criteria come from the provider: the order says wean by 0.02 mcg/kg/min every 15-30 minutes when MAP is over 75, and Dr. Brandt's plan (2345) says once MAP is 70 or higher and lactate under 2. The first step down at 0000 was made with MAP 74-75 and lactate 2.6 (falling; 1.8 at 0200); accept any answer that names a MAP above goal with a falling lactate. The nurse weans only per the provider's order, one small step at a time, and stops and calls if the MAP drops under 65.

Recheck MAP every 15 minutes for the first hour, then hourly (done after 0430: MAP 77, 75, 76); heart rate, urine output, capillary refill/skin temperature, mental status, temperature and the next lactate; hydrocortisone continues. Call Dr. Brandt for MAP under 65, a rising heart rate, falling urine output, cool mottled skin or a rising lactate: the pressor may need to restart; keep the central line and the drug available.

items.title: The Kidneys, the Vancomycin Level and Procalcitonin
items.prompt: Open Lab Results (Creatinine, Vancomycin level, Procalcitonin) and the pharmacy note. (a) Write the creatinine at 1700, 2300 and 0500 and say what change this is (and whether his urine output agrees). (b) Why does the combination of vancomycin and piperacillin-tazobactam worry the pharmacist?
