(c) The vancomycin level of 11.6 was drawn at 0415: why is it drawn before the 0430 dose, and what question do you ask? (d) What does procalcitonin 9.6 add?
items.where: Lab Results (Chemistry, Drug levels, Procalcitonin); Chart Review > Notes (Pharmacy 1930, Nursing Notes 0300 and 0450); Intake/Output

elements.t: Creatinine 1.1 (1700) -> 1.3 (2300) -> 1.4 (0500; baseline about 1.0): a rise of 0.3 mg/dL in 12 hours = acute kidney injury, stage 1 (KDIGO); BUN 27 -> 30. Urine output actually improved (0.34 mL/kg/h at 1900-2000 to 0.79 at 0500-0600), so it is a non-oliguric injury; likely sepsis/hypoperfusion plus nephrotoxic drugs.

Vancomycin plus pip-tazo is associated with more AKI than either drug alone; both depend on the kidneys, so a falling clearance makes levels rise; pharmacy will reassess vancomycin when the culture returns (if MSSA, a beta-lactam).

Drugs with a narrow safe range are checked by levels; the level is drawn at 0415, 15 minutes before the dose, so it shows the lowest concentration and clearance (11.6; pharmacy uses AUC dosing, not a trough alone). Draw it on time, and ask pharmacy/provider to review the 0430 dose of 1,250 mg in light of the rising creatinine (1.3 at 2300) before or after it runs; avoid NSAIDs, contrast and other nephrotoxins; strict urine output.

Procalcitonin 9.6 ng/mL (4.8 at 1555): high, a marker of severe bacterial infection and sepsis; it supports the diagnosis and the trend is used later to decide when to stop antibiotics; it does not identify the organism.

items.title: The Night Shift Intake and Output
items.prompt: Open the Intake/Output flowsheet (Totals) and the albumin order. (a) Write the totals for "Night shift 11/03 1900 to 11/04 0700" and the net balance, and (use the printed shift total, not your own sum of the hourly rows; ignore the later day-shift row) and compare the weight at 0400 (91.2 kg) with the admission weight (82 kg). (b) The output for 0200-0300 is 280 mL: how much is urine and what is the rest? (c) Albumin 5% 500 mL ran 2200 to 0200: what mL/h is that, why was it given, and what do you watch for?
items.where: Flowsheets > Intake/Output (shift totals, hourly rows); Flowsheets (Daily weight, Bowel); MAR (albumin); Orders

elements.t: Intake 4,160 mL, output 803 mL, net +3,357 mL (4,160 - 803). Weight 91.2 kg vs 82 kg = +9.2 kg (about 11% above admission): fluid (edema 2-3+) from the capillary leak; watch lungs, ventilator pressures, edema, bladder pressure.

Only 60 mL of the 280 mL at 0200-0300 is urine; the rest (220 mL) is a loose stool (tube-feeding related), so do not call it a diuresis. Real urine output improved from 28 mL/h (1900-2000, 0.34 mL/kg/h) to 68 mL/h (0600-0700, 0.83 mL/kg/h).

500 mL / 4 h = 125 mL/h. Albumin 5% is a colloid: it draws and holds fluid in the vessels, supports the pressure and urine output in septic shock and burn leak with less crystalloid (LR was lowered to 75 mL/h at 0200). Watch for fluid overload: crackles, rising peak/plateau pressures, SpO2, edema, CVP, and for a BP rise.

items.title: Handoff at 0650
items.prompt: It is 0650 on Wednesday. Write your SBAR handoff for J. Morales, RN, the day nurse. Use real numbers, the events of the night, what is due in the next hours (look at the MAR and Orders), and anything you want the day team to follow up.
items.where: Everything you read and charted this night; Orders; MAR; Lab Results; Flowsheets

elements.t: Situation: Marcus Delaney, BICU-6, full code, NKDA, contact precautions; burn wound septic shock (MSSA suspected), now improving; off norepinephrine since 0430 (MAP 75-77); intubated.

Background: 22% TBSA flame burn with inhalation injury, hospital day 3; cultures 1550 Tuesday before pip-tazo and vancomycin; hydrocortisone 50 mg q6h since 2030; wound Gram stain GPC in clusters (2130) and blood culture bottle positive GPC in clusters at 0240 (identification pending); left IJ line day 3, site clean.

Assessment: T 100.2 (from 102.4), HR 101, BP 110/59 (MAP 76), RR 19, SpO2 97%; vent AC/VC 450, RR 16, PEEP 5, FiO2 0.40 since 0600; lactate 4.1 -> 1.5; WBC 19.2 (bands 9%), platelets 128, creatinine 1.4 (peak), PCT 9.6, vancomycin level 11.6; UOP 65 mL/h (0.79 mL/kg/h); glucose 175 on insulin 1.5 units/h; propofol 30, fentanyl 100, RASS -2, CPOT 1; I&O +3,357; weight 91.2 kg.

Recommendation: MAP every hour and call for under 65; SAT/SBT at 0800; hydrocortisone and pip-tazo due 0830; mafenide soak due about 0930 with premedication; follow creatinine, urine output, platelets and glucose (hourly; hypoglycemia risk as insulin needs fall); pharmacy review of vancomycin; ID/burn team about the culture and the line; wean sedation/FiO2; acetaminophen next 1400 (LFTs); family updated, phone numbers on file.

parts.title: Shift 5: Wednesday 11/04 0700 to 1900 (day shift)
parts.intro: Set the simulation clock to 0700 on Wednesday 11/04/26. You are J. Morales, RN, the day nurse: Marcus is recovering from the burn-wound sepsis, off norepinephrine since 0430, and is due for the sedation break and breathing trial. Keep reading forward in the chart as the clock moves; do not look past 1900 for this shift.
parts.keyNote: Shift 5 is the recovery day: weaning from the ventilator, the first hours after extubation, reading microbiology and narrowing antibiotics, moving from IV infusions to oral care, and a handoff. A careful student should earn about 12 of the 16 points. Notes on chart quirks: the microbiology results are filed in the Lab Results grid under the time each became available (MSSA at 1500, urine and repeat cultures at 1600); the I&O day-shift totals are those shown in the EHR (1,823 / 836 / +987).

items.title: The 0800 Sedation Break and the 0930 Breathing Trial
items.prompt: Read the 0820 nursing note, the 0955 respiratory therapy note and the SBT order. (a) What does a PASSED daily sedation interruption (SAT) look like, and what did Marcus show (RASS, CAM-ICU, pain, vital signs)? Which sedative was turned off and which continued? What would a FAILED SAT look like and what do you do? (b) Describe the spontaneous breathing trial (settings and length), then CALCULATE the RSBI from the respiratory rate and the exhaled tidal volume in the RT note and compare it with the pass value. (c) What did the cuff-leak test show and why is it done in a patient with an inhalation injury?
items.where: Chart Review > Notes (0820 Nursing Note, 0955 RT Note); Orders (SBT, SAT); Flowsheets (RASS, CPOT, ventilator)

elements.t: Passed SAT: wakes to voice within minutes and stays calm and comfortable: RASS 0 (goal 0 to -1), follows commands (left hand, toes, nods), CPOT 0/8, CAM-ICU NEGATIVE, HR 90s, MAP 76-78, RR 17-18, SpO2 98%, no dyssynchrony. Propofol turned off at 0800; fentanyl 100 mcg/h continued for pain.

Failed SAT: sustained agitation or anxiety, pain not controlled, RR over 35 or distress, SpO2 under 88-90%, new arrhythmia or ischemia, or a rising HR/BP. Action: stop the test, treat pain and distress, restart the sedative at HALF the previous rate (order), notify the provider, and try again the next day.

SBT: pressure support 5 / PEEP 5 / FiO2 0.35 for 30 minutes (0925/0930 to 0955) with RT. RSBI = RR / VT in liters = 18 / 0.310 L = about 58 breaths/min/L (accept 56-60); pass is under 105. Other pass criteria met: RR under 30, SpO2 97%, HR change under 5% (limit 20%), no distress.

Cuff leak: audible leak, measured about 190 mL (more than 110 mL). A leak around the deflated cuff means the airway is not swollen shut; it is done because inhalation injury and 2 days of fluid resuscitation cause upper-airway edema, and without a leak there is a high risk of stridor and reintubation after extubation. (Still a concern in this patient even with a leak.)

items.title: Reading the Breathing Graph Before and After Extubation
items.prompt: The graph shows respiratory rate, SpO2 and heart rate from the flowsheet, Wednesday 0400 to 1200 (the dotted line is 30 breaths/min). He was extubated at 1045. (a) Looking only at 0600 to 1000, what does the graph show about his readiness to come off the ventilator? Use numbers. (b) What changes on the graph after 1045, give the values, and explain why this is or is not worrying. (c) Which graph changes would make you call the provider and RT, and what would you do at the bedside while waiting?
items.where: Flowsheets > Vital Signs (RR, SpO2, HR); Chart Review > Extubation Procedure Note and 1250 Nursing Note (ABG 1200)

images.caption: Figure: Respiratory rate, SpO2 and heart rate, Wednesday 11/04/26, 0400 to 1200 (from the flowsheet). Dotted line = 30 breaths/min.

elements.t: Ready: from 0600 to 1000 the respiratory rate is steady and low (17-19), well under the 30 line; SpO2 is 97-99% on FiO2 0.40 then 0.35; heart rate is falling and settled (101 -> 93). No tachypnea, desaturation or tachycardia (the breathing trial was at 0925-0955, between the 0900 and 1000 points), so he is stable on minimal support (consistent with passing the SBT).

After 1045: RR rises from 18 to 20, 22 and 23 (plateau 23 at 1115-1200), SpO2 falls from 99% to 96-97%, HR 95 -> 91 (not rising). Expected and acceptable: he now breathes without ventilator pressure support or PEEP, has a sore, hoarse throat and is anxious, and gets 4 L nasal cannula (about 0.36 FiO2). It plateaued (RR still under 30, SpO2 at or above 92%, HR not rising), the ABG at 1200 was pH 7.39, PaCO2 41, PaO2 88, and there was no stridor or accessory muscle use at 1100 (the 1200 flowsheet notes only mild increased effort, hoarse voice, no stridor). Keep trending.

Call for: RR continuing up toward or over 30 (or a steady climb), SpO2 under 92% despite more oxygen, a rising heart rate, stridor, accessory muscle use or tiring, falling mental status. At the bedside: stay with him, sit him upright (HOB 45 degrees or more), check airway sounds and work of breathing, increase O2 as ordered, call RT and Dr. Brandt, have suction, bag-valve mask and the reintubation kit ready.

items.title: Right After the Tube Comes Out (1045)
items.prompt: Open the 1100 Extubation Procedure Note and your 1130 nursing note. (a) List FOUR things you assess in the first hour after extubation (and how often) and what you found at 1050-1115. Why is he at higher risk for airway swelling than another patient? (b) If STRIDOR develops, what do you do and what does the provider plan say to give? (c) Why must the airway watch continue even though he looks well at 1100?
items.where: Chart Review > Notes (1100 Extubation Procedure Note, 1130 Nursing Note, 0955 RT Note); Orders; MAR

elements.t: Any four: stridor (high-pitched sound on breathing in), voice quality (hoarse but phonating is expected), work of breathing (accessory muscles, retractions, nasal flaring), RR, SpO2, HR/BP, cough strength and secretions, drooling or swallowing, mental status. Plan: vitals and airway assessment every 15 minutes for 1 hour, then hourly, continuous SpO2 and cardiac monitor. Findings: hoarse voice, weak but effective cough, no stridor, no drooling, no accessory muscle use, RR 20-23, SpO2 96-97% on 4 L.
Higher risk: grade 2 inhalation injury (swelling of the airway lining from smoke), about 56 hours of intubation (laryngeal trauma) and 2 days of large-volume resuscitation (edema).

Stridor: stay with him, sit him up, call RT and Dr. Brandt immediately (reintubation readiness), give oxygen, keep suction, bag-valve mask and reintubation equipment (8.0 and 7.0 tubes, video laryngoscope) at the bedside. Ordered treatment: racemic epinephrine 2.25% 0.5 mL in 3 mL saline by nebulizer, repeat every 20 minutes up to 3 times; heliox if available; hydrocortisone continues. Watch for a rising heart rate from the epinephrine and for swelling returning when it wears off. Keep NPO.

items.title: Dexmedetomidine After Extubation
items.prompt: Dexmedetomidine was started at 1100. Open the order. (a) Calculate the pump rate in mL/h (weight 82 kg, bag 4 mcg/mL, dose 0.4 mcg/kg/h). (b) When do you hold it and notify the provider according to the ORDER? (c) The surgeon wrote "avoid benzodiazepines": give two reasons that a drug like dexmedetomidine suits this patient better than lorazepam.
items.where: Orders and MAR (dexmedetomidine); Chart Review > 1100 and 1130 Notes; Flowsheets (HR, BP, RASS)

elements.t: 0.4 mcg/kg/h x 82 kg = 32.8 mcg/h; 32.8 / 4 mcg/mL = 8.2 mL/h.

Hold and notify for HR under 50 or SBP under 90 (as written in the order; the 1130 nursing note lists HR under 50 or MAP under 65: confirm against the order). Titrate 0.1 mcg/kg/h to RASS 0 to -1. Expected effects are bradycardia and hypotension: HR stayed 88-94 and MAP 78-81 for the rest of the shift.

Any two: keeps him calm yet arousable and breathing on his own (little respiratory depression, important right after extubation); benzodiazepines raise the risk of delirium and prolong confusion in the ICU (CAM-ICU was negative and we want it to stay that way); benzodiazepines blunt his cough and breathing drive and add to opioids; Dr. Okafor and the ICU plan avoid them.

items.title: NPO, the OG Tube, Breathing Exercises and Nausea
items.prompt: After extubation he was NPO, the OG tube was removed at 1115, and at about 1215 he felt nauseated; ondansetron 4 mg IV was given at 1230. (a) Why NPO until the swallow screen, and why was the OG tube taken out now? (b) What do you do for incentive spirometry and oral care? (c) For the nausea: what do you do first, what is the safe-practice trap, and what do you check about the drug?
items.where: Orders (Diet, Aspiration precautions); MAR (ondansetron); Chart Review > 1130 and 1250 Nursing Notes, 1230 Nutrition Note

elements.t: NPO: after 56 hours of intubation the swallow and cough are weak, so food, water or saliva can go into the lungs (aspiration pneumonia); the screen is ordered before anything by mouth. OG tube out: feeds were stopped at 1030 and it is no longer needed once extubated; the tube sits across the throat and swallowing muscles, increases reflux and aspiration, irritates the nose and throat and is uncomfortable; he is awake. (He is NPO, so medicines are IV until the screen.)

Incentive spirometer hourly while awake (slow deep breath, hold 3-5 seconds, about 10 times, then cough; coached to about 1,000 mL) to prevent atelectasis; HOB 45 degrees; oral care with swabs and a moist mouth because he cannot drink (reduces bacteria that could be aspirated).

Nausea: sit him upright, check airway, suction ready, assess for cause (pain, swallowed secretions, anxiety), give ondansetron 4 mg IV PRN (order every 8 hours); no sips, ice chips or crackers for nausea because he is NPO until the screen (the trap); reassess in 30 minutes (improved at 1245). Check QTc/other QT-prolonging drugs and last dose time before giving.

items.title: The Insulin Infusion Ends at Noon: Reading the Correction Scale
items.prompt: Open the glucose results, the insulin lispro correction-scale order and the MAR. (a) His glucose values from 0930 to 1800 and why the infusion was stopped at 1200. (b) Using the ORDER, how many units of lispro would you give for glucose 149, 162, 238, 276 and 362, and when do you call the provider? (c) Name one safety concern in the hours around the change (feeds stopped, hydrocortisone dropped to 25 mg) and how often glucose is checked now.
items.where: Lab Results (Glucose, point of care and serum); Orders (insulin lispro correction scale); MAR; Notes (1230 Nutrition note)

elements.t: POC glucose 162 (0930), 154 (1030), 150 (1130), 149 (1800); serum 147 at 1700. The infusion (1 unit/h) was stopped at 1200 because glucose was stable around 150 (goal 140-180), the tube feeds had been off since 1030, the sepsis was resolving and the steroid dose was being reduced; he moves to subcutaneous correction insulin.

Scale: 151-200 = 2 units; 201-250 = 4; 251-300 = 6; 301-350 = 8; over 350 = 10 units AND call the provider. So 149 = 0 units (below the first row), 162 = 2 units, 238 = 4 units, 276 = 6 units, 362 = 10 units plus call. Under 70: treat per hypoglycemia protocol and call. Check the glucose first, pick the row that contains it, and read the number carefully (150 and 149 get no insulin).

Concern: NPO or poor intake with insulin on board can cause hypoglycemia (feeds off since 1030, infusion still running until 1200; hydrocortisone being tapered lowers insulin need). Glucose is checked every 6 hours while NPO, then before meals and at bedtime once he eats (soft diet 1800); give correction insulin with the meal, not alone; watch for low-sugar signs.

items.title: The 1330 Family Meeting
items.prompt: Read the Case Management family meeting note (the meeting was at 1330). (a) Give two things Dr. Okafor told the family about the next days. (b) The patient was not in the room: what happened afterwards, and give one thing you as the bedside nurse can do to support Marcus and his family after the meeting.
items.where: Chart Review > Notes (Case Management Family Meeting Note, 1430)

elements.t: Any two: continue burn ICU care 1-2 more days then burn step-down; excision and skin grafting tentatively Friday 11/06 (right forearm, hand and chest) with grafts from his own thigh; hospital stay about 2-4 weeks; prognosis good for survival, hand function depends on early therapy; rehab vs home with outpatient burn clinic decided after surgery; Full Code confirmed.

Dr. Okafor updated Marcus at the bedside afterwards and he agreed with the plan; consent for surgery is to be completed with the patient (not the family) on Thursday. Nurse support: reinforce the information in plain words, answer questions or relay them to the team, encourage the family to rest, support splint/exercise teaching, child life and social work (Ava), document the meeting and the patient's understanding.

items.title: The 1400 Dressing Change with Mafenide
items.prompt: Read the 1430 nursing note and the MAR. (a) When and what did you give before the dressing change, and why that timing? He still reported 6/10: what else do you do? (b) Why is mafenide used for this wound, and what two problems do you watch for with mafenide (find the numbers that show whether the second one is happening)? (c) Name four things you assess and document about the wound at this change, using what the note found (and why the marker line matters). (d) What precautions apply?
items.where: MAR (hydromorphone 1345, mafenide, acetaminophen); Orders (burn wound care); Lab Results (CO2/bicarbonate, ABG 1200); Chart Review > 1430 Nursing Note

elements.t: Hydromorphone 0.5 mg IV at 1345, 15 minutes before the 1400 change so the IV peak effect (about 10-20 min) covers the pain; scheduled acetaminophen 1 g IV at 1400. Pain was 6/10 during, 4/10 after. Also: coach slow breathing, pause when asked (paused twice), warm/gentle technique, reassess 30 minutes after, sedation level (RASS) because of dexmedetomidine and opioid together.

Mafenide 5% soaks penetrate eschar, so they work on a deep wound infection (MSSA under the eschar) where silver sulfadiazine did not. Watch for (1) severe burning pain on application, and (2) metabolic acidosis because it inhibits carbonic anhydrase (also rash, hyperventilation). Numbers: bicarbonate 22 at 0500 and 24 at 1700, anion gap 9, ABG 1200 pH 7.39 / HCO3 24, RR not increasing, so no acidosis. Next soaks 1730; BMP every 12 h.

Any four: drainage amount and character (thin serosanguineous, no pus), odor (much less), erythema margin versus the skin-marker line from Tuesday 1430 (not extending: a spread means worsening infection), eschar edge (still separating at the right chest border), the violaceous area (unchanged, surgeon evaluating), face, right hand (Doppler signals, cap refill), photographs and measurements.

Contact precautions with the burn nurse (N. Ibarra): gown and gloves for all wound care (per the order; add mask or eye protection if splash is likely, per unit policy), clean or sterile technique per unit policy; splint reapplied after.

items.title: Reading the Culture Results in the Lab Section
items.prompt: The picture shows the Microbiology rows of Lab Results at 1630 Wednesday (cultures were drawn Tuesday at 1550). (a) For the wound culture, the blood cultures (4 bottles), the tracheal aspirate, the urine culture and the repeat blood cultures, write what each shows and the time column it appears under. Is any result still not final? (b) The rows for blood culture set 1, set 2 and the wound Gram stain look empty: why, and where would you scroll to find their results? (c) The lab called at 1500: what does "MSSA in 2 of 4 bottles" tell you (true infection or contaminant?) and what does it NOT yet tell you? (d) What does "no growth to date" on the repeat blood cultures mean at 1630?
items.where: Lab Results > Microbiology (newest columns at the right; scroll left for the 11/03 1550 and 11/04 0240 entries); Chart Review > 1540 Pharmacy Note

images.caption: Figure: Lab Results review, Microbiology and Bedside Testing rows, 11/04/26 at 1630 (columns 0930 to 1600).

elements.t: 1500 column: wound culture = Staphylococcus aureus (MSSA) identified, susceptibilities to follow (NOT final); blood cultures (4 bottles) = MSSA in 2 of 4 bottles (one peripheral, one central line), preliminary; tracheal aspirate = normal respiratory flora, few WBC. 1600 column: urine culture = no growth at 24 hours (preliminary); repeat blood cultures = collected, no growth to date. Still pending: wound susceptibilities (and the final blood culture panel).

The grid files each result under the time it became available. Set 1, set 2 and the Gram stain only have entries earlier: the Tuesday 1550 columns (collected, in process), Tuesday 2130 (wound Gram stain: many WBC, GPC in clusters) and Wednesday 0240 (set 2 central line bottle 1 of 4 positive at 10 hours, GPC in clusters, critical call). Scroll left to see them. The four-bottle result replaces them at 1500.

S. aureus in blood from two sets (one peripheral) is a true bacteremia, never treated as a contaminant; the wound is the likely source (clean line site). "Methicillin-sensitive" means beta-lactams work. It does not yet give the final susceptibility panel (which antibiotics; wound culture susceptibilities still pending) and does not show clearance or whether the line is infected.

"Collected, no growth to date" 30 minutes after collection only means nothing has grown YET (cultures take 24-48 hours to call; a 24-hour no-growth result would be expected Thursday afternoon); it is not proof of clearance.

items.title: MSSA: Narrowing the Antibiotics, Repeat Cultures and the Central Line
items.prompt: Read the 1145 ID consult, the 1540 pharmacy note, the Orders and the 1645 nursing note. (a) Vancomycin was stopped at 1530: why, and which antibiotic is better for MSSA? (b) Why does narrowing antibiotics matter, and why is pip-tazo still running? (c) What did ID ask for about repeat blood cultures: how many, from where, when (you drew them at 1600 before the 1630 pip-tazo), and for how long will he need antibiotics? (d) What is the decision about the left IJ central line and what would change it? What do you do for the line meanwhile?
items.where: Chart Review > Notes (1145 ID Consultation, 1540 Pharmacy Stewardship Note, 1645 Nursing Note); Orders (vancomycin, cefazolin, pip-tazo, repeat blood cultures); MAR

elements.t: Vancomycin stopped 1530 because the organism is MSSA, not MRSA; vancomycin is inferior to a beta-lactam for MSSA, and vancomycin plus pip-tazo is nephrotoxic (creatinine peaked 1.4). Better drug: cefazolin 2 g IV q8h (ordered 1640 by Dr. Raman, first dose 0610 Thursday).

Narrowing = stewardship: use the most effective, narrowest drug; reduces kidney injury and side effects, C. difficile, resistant organisms and gut flora damage, and the drug that kills MSSA best gives better outcomes. Pip-tazo continues (0830, 1630, 0030) as a bridge for possible Gram-negative or mixed burn-wound flora until wound and biopsy cultures are final; then it is stopped.

Two sets (one peripheral, one from the central line) at 1600 before the next antibiotic dose, repeated every 24-48 hours until negative. If uncomplicated MSSA bacteremia with a controlled source and clearance: at least 14 days of IV therapy counted from the first NEGATIVE culture (longer, 4-6 weeks, if complicated); excision and grafting Friday is source control.

Line stays for now (wound is the likely source, clean site, he needs central access, it is his only IV after 1800). Remove and replace at a new site if repeat cultures stay positive at 48-72 hours, the site becomes infected, or he becomes unstable again; TTE if cultures stay positive. Meanwhile: daily necessity review, check the site every shift, chlorhexidine dressing, scrub the hub 15 seconds, aseptic technique, report fever or redness.

items.title: First Time Out of Bed with PT and OT
items.prompt: Read the 1520 PT note, the 1535 OT note and the OOB order. (a) What do you watch and measure during the first dangle, stand and chair transfer, and when do you stop? (b) Give three safe-handling points for the lines and the burned right arm. (c) What are the splint instructions from OT?
items.where: Orders (Activity); Chart Review > PT Note 1520 and OT Note 1535; Flowsheets (HR, SpO2)

elements.t: Monitor HR, BP, RR, SpO2 and symptoms before, during and after (dizziness, fatigue, pain, shortness of breath); dangle and chair findings: HR 98, SpO2 95%, RR 22, mild dizziness that resolved in 2 minutes; after: HR 91, SpO2 96%, BP 112/64. Stop and return him to bed for SpO2 under 92%, HR over 130, drop in BP, chest pain, marked dizziness or distress. Premedicate 30-45 minutes before.

Any three: 2-person assist with a gait belt; RN manages the lines (left IJ, left radial A-line, left AC PIV, Foley) so nothing pulls; log-roll avoiding the burned chest and arm; right arm supported on a pillow or trough above heart level; bed alarm, non-skid socks, fall precautions (weak legs, sedating drugs); oxygen on; not during the dressing change window.

Resting hand splint in position of function (wrist 20-30 degrees extension, MCP 70-90 flexion, IP extended, thumb abducted); on at all times except dressing change and therapy; check skin under the straps every shift for pressure; reapply after the mafenide soaks; gentle finger movements hourly while awake; elevate the arm.

items.title: The Swallow Screen, Diet and the New Pain Pills
items.prompt: At 1600 he passed the bedside swallow screen and the soft diet started at 1800. (a) What did the screen include and what are your aspiration precautions? When do you stop the meal? (b) You give oxycodone 5 mg at 1645: why 5 mg, and what do you check first (look at the order and the other sedating drugs)? (c) Gabapentin 300 mg three times daily was also ordered: why, and what do you watch for?
items.where: Chart Review > 1610 SLP Note, 1645 Nursing Note; Orders (Diet, oxycodone, gabapentin); MAR

elements.t: Screen: alert and upright, oral exam, ice chips, teaspoons then 3 oz (90 mL) water without cough, wet voice or desaturation (SpO2 95-96%), puree and soft solid. Soft diet with thin liquids and supplements. Precautions: upright 90 degrees for meals and 30 minutes after, small bites and slow sips, supervised first meals, no straws at first, oral care before and after. Stop and call for cough, wet voice, stridor, increased work of breathing or SpO2 under 92%.

Order: 5 mg for pain 4-6, 10 mg for 7-10; his pain was 4/10, so 5 mg. Check RASS and RR first: hold for RASS -2 or lower or RR under 10 (high-alert opioid); it adds to dexmedetomidine and gabapentin (sedation, respiratory depression), so reassess sedation and breathing 30-60 minutes later; give for pain after the screen so he can swallow it with puree.

Gabapentin: for burn neuropathic pain and itch (spares opioid); causes sedation, dizziness and fall risk, adds to the other sedatives, dose adjusted for kidney function (creatinine 1.2, CrCl about 100). Watch RASS, dizziness when he stands, fall precautions; pharmacy advises holding for RASS -2 or lower.

items.title: Wednesday Labs: Is the Infection Getting Better?
items.prompt: Open Lab Results and look at the creatinine, WBC (with bands) and procalcitonin from Tuesday afternoon through the 1700 draw on Wednesday. Write the values for each and what each trend tells you about his kidneys and the infection.
items.where: Lab Results (Chemistry: Creatinine, BUN; CBC; Inflammatory: Procalcitonin)

elements.t: Creatinine 1.1 (Tue 1700) -> 1.3 (2300) -> 1.4 (Wed 0500, peak; mild AKI, KDIGO stage 1 from shock plus vancomycin and pip-tazo) -> 1.2 (Wed 1700): improving as perfusion recovered and urine output is about 70 mL/h; BUN 30 -> 24. Keep avoiding nephrotoxins (NSAIDs, contrast).
WBC 18.4 (Tue 1555) -> 21.8 (2100, bands 14%) -> 19.2 (0500, bands 9%) -> 15.6 (Wed 1700, bands 4%): falling, fewer immature cells: the body is responding to treatment and source control.

Procalcitonin 4.8 (Tue 1555) -> 9.6 (Wed 0400, peak) -> 6.1 (Wed 1600): rose after the sepsis started and is now coming down, which supports a responding infection (it lags); it does not replace the wound exam, temperature and cultures; keep trending daily.

items.title: Intake and Output: Where Did the Fluid Go?
items.prompt: Open the Intake/Output flowsheet. The Day shift 11/04 0700 to 1900 total is intake 1,823 mL, output 836 mL, net +987 mL. (a) Calculate his average urine output in mL/h and mL/kg/h (82 kg) and compare it with the Parkland goal of 0.5 mL/kg/h. (b) Why is the urine output high now, and why is the net still positive although the fluids were cut (LR 75 -> 50 mL/h at 1200, stopped at 1800)? (c) What would you watch or ask the team about next?
items.where: Intake/Output flowsheet (Totals and hourly entries); Orders; Flowsheets > Cardiac; MAR (LR rate changes)

elements.t: 836 mL / 12 h = about 70 mL/h; 70 / 82 = about 0.85 mL/kg/h (accept 0.8-0.9), well above the 0.5 mL/kg/h (41 mL/h) goal; net 1,823 - 836 = +987.

Capillary leak is closing and the shocked kidneys have recovered: the fluid that went into the tissues (edema; the stay so far is about +17 liters) moves back into the vessels and is excreted (mobilization phase); less LR and normal kidney perfusion allow diuresis. Net is still positive because intake (IV carrier, LR, feeds until 1030, first oral intake at 1800-1900) still exceeds output, and insensible losses and the open burn wounds are not measured. The net is much smaller than the +3,357 on the night shift.

Watch: urine hourly with the Foley (still needed), daily weight (91.2 kg by bed scale at 0400, up from 82 kg on admission; not rechecked on the day shift), lung sounds and oxygen need, edema, creatinine/BMP, potassium and magnesium (loss with diuresis), blood pressure; ask whether the Foley is still needed and whether any fluid is wanted once he eats and drinks. Call for a drop below 0.5 mL/kg/h (about 41 mL/h) or a rise in creatinine.

items.title: Handoff at 1850
items.prompt: It is 1850 on Wednesday. Write your SBAR handoff for E. Haddad, RN, the night nurse. Use real numbers from the chart, include what happened today, what the night nurse must do or watch in the next hours (look at the MAR and orders), and the things still pending.
items.where: Everything you read and charted this shift; Orders; MAR; Lab Results; Flowsheets; Intake/Output

elements.t: Situation: Marcus Delaney, BICU-6, Full Code, NKDA, contact precautions; 22% TBSA burn with inhalation injury, MSSA sepsis from the wounds resolving; extubated 1045 and stable on 2 L nasal cannula: 1800 T 99.0, HR 90, BP 113/65 (MAP 81), RR 21, SpO2 96%, pain 4/10, RASS 0.

Background: off norepinephrine since 0430, SAT and SBT passed (RSBI 58), no stridor; MSSA in 2 of 4 blood bottles and wound at 1500; vancomycin stopped 1530; pip-tazo continues, cefazolin 2 g IV q8h starts 0610 Thursday; repeat blood cultures drawn 1600; swallow screen passed 1600, soft diet at 1800; left AC PIV out and LR off at 1800, saline 20 mL/h via the left IJ (only access); insulin infusion stopped 1200 and lispro scale.

Assessment: day shift intake 1,823, output 836 (about 70 mL/h), net +987; labs 1700: WBC 15.6, bands 4%, creatinine 1.2 (from 1.4), K 4.2, glucose 147; PCT 6.1; glucose 149 at 1800 (no insulin needed); pain 4/10 on acetaminophen IV, oxycodone 5 mg at 1645; dexmedetomidine 0.4 mcg/kg/h with HR 88-91, no bradycardia; wound: drainage down, erythema within the marker; right hand Doppler present; dinner tray pending.

Recommendation / to do: mafenide soaks 1730 done, next 0130; hydrocortisone 25 mg 2030; pip-tazo 0030; first oral doses incl. gabapentin; watch for stridor/hoarseness and aspiration with meals (upright, supervised); glucose before meals and bedtime with the scale; hourly IS; sedation and falls (assist x2); follow repeat blood cultures, wound culture final and the surgery plan (OR Friday: consent with Jenna present, NPO per surgery); keep dexmedetomidine hold parameters; monitor temperature and creatinine.

parts.title: Shift 6: Wednesday 11/04 1900 to Thursday 11/05 0700 (night shift)
parts.step: Recovery and transfer out of the ICU
parts.intro: Set the simulation clock to 1900 on Wednesday 11/04/26. You take report from J. Morales, RN, and care for Marcus until you hand him off to the Med-Surg nurse at 0650 on Thursday 11/05. Keep reading forward in the chart as the clock moves; do not look past 0700 for this shift.
parts.keyNote: Shift 6 is the quiet night of recovery: oral pain control and the nutrition plan, a delirium and withdrawal watch after sedation is off, the change to targeted antibiotics, the removal of the arterial line and Foley, and the decision that he is ready to leave the ICU. The graph and the transfer SBAR bring the whole stay together. A careful student should earn about 12 of the 16 points.

items.title: Vital Signs Through the Last Night
items.where: Flowsheets > Vital Signs
items.prompt: Set the clock to 1900 on Wednesday 11/04. Copy the vital signs at each time and circle every abnormal value. Then write two sentences below: (1) what changed in his breathing support and pain across the night, and (2) one thing the vital signs cannot tell you about the infection.

key.rules: Score 0.75 x (cells correct / 24), rounded to the nearest 0.25. The two sentences are worth 0.25 (item 6.1b): (1) oxygen was 2 L/min nasal cannula until it was weaned to room air at 0300 (SpO2 95-96% throughout); pain fell from 4/10 (1900) to 3/10 (2100 on) on oxycodone, gabapentin and acetaminophen; (2) vital signs cannot show what the wound looks like (purulent drainage, odor, spreading erythema), the white count and procalcitonin, or whether the blood cultures are clearing; a normal temperature can also be masked by scheduled acetaminophen. Chart values: T 99.0, 98.9, 98.7, 98.8; HR 89, 87, 84, 82; BP 110/63, 113/64, 114/66, 112/64; RR 20, 19, 19, 18; SpO2 95, 96, 96, 96; pain 4, 3, 3, 3. Everything is in the normal range except the pain score and the low-grade temperature of 99.0 (accept "no abnormal values" with pain circled). Allow +/- 2 for rates and +/- 0.2 F.

items.title: Two sentences for item 6.1
items.prompt: (1) What changed in his breathing support and pain across the night? (2) One thing the vital signs cannot tell you about the infection.
items.where: Flowsheets > Vital Signs

elements.t: Both sentences correct: (1) 2 L nasal cannula to room air at 0300 with SpO2 96% and pain 4 to 3/10; (2) vital signs do not show the wound, WBC/procalcitonin or the cultures (acetaminophen can mask a fever).

items.title: Soft Diet and the Correction Scale
items.prompt: Marcus eats a soft diet with shakes and the insulin infusion is off. (a) Read the dinner intake in the 2000 flowsheet and the glucose values at 1800, 0000 and 0600; using the lispro correction scale order, how many units were due for each? (b) The last hydrocortisone dose was at 0230: how will that change his glucose, and why is the risk of low glucose still small on this scale? (c) He eats only about half of each tray: name two actions for his nutrition before Friday's surgery.
items.where: Flowsheets > GI (Diet / Feeding); Lab Results (Glucose, point of care); Orders (insulin lispro correction scale, soft diet); Intake/Output

elements.t: Dinner: ate 50% of the soft tray. Glucose 149 (1800), 141 (0000), 141 (0600); the scale gives 2 units only for 151-200 (4 units for 201-250), so 0 units each time (none were given on the MAR).

Stopping hydrocortisone (stress-dose steroids raise glucose) means glucose should drift DOWN over the next day; the risk of hypoglycemia is small because only a correction scale (no basal insulin) is ordered and glucose is 141; recheck before meals/bedtime and treat under 70 per protocol; ask the provider whether to hold the scale when NPO after midnight Thursday.

Any two: calorie count and record the percent of each meal; offer the high-protein shakes TID (ordered); help him sit upright to eat (aspiration precautions, 90 degrees); small frequent snacks; dietitian follow-up for higher calories/protein for wound healing and the donor site; vitamin C and zinc per MAR.

items.title: Pain and Sleep Now That He Is Awake
items.prompt: Open the 2230 and 0315 nursing notes, the pain flowsheet and the MAR. (a) Which pain scale do you use now, and why is the CPOT no longer the right tool? Give his scores at rest and with turning or the soaks. (b) List the doses of oxycodone, gabapentin and acetaminophen he received overnight with times. At 0130 mafenide soaks hurt (5/10) and the oxycodone was given at 0215: what would you do differently for the next soak at 0930? (c) At 0615 you are about to give the acetaminophen tablet: what must you check on the MAR and the order before giving it, and what is his daily limit? (d) Name two ways you protected his sleep and one safety check you make after giving oxycodone with gabapentin.
items.where: Chart Review > Notes (Nursing Note 2230, 0315); Flowsheets > Pain; MAR; Orders (acetaminophen, oxycodone, gabapentin)

elements.t: Numeric 0-10 self-report scale, because he is awake (RASS 0), oriented and able to report; CPOT is for patients who cannot self-report (intubated or sedated). Scores: 4/10 at 1900, 3/10 at rest from 2100, 5/10 with turning and the soak (up to 6/10 with care).

Oxycodone 5 mg at 2100, 0215 and 0615; gabapentin 300 mg at 2200 and 0620; acetaminophen 1 g IV at 2200, then 1,000 mg tablet at 0615. Next time give the oxycodone 30-45 minutes BEFORE the 0930 soak (Dr. Okafor's plan), not after the pain starts.

Check that no other acetaminophen is due or already given: the IV order ended at 0500 and the tablet order starts at 0600 (give only ONE form); last dose 2200 (more than 8 h ago); total in the last 24 h is 3 g (1400, 2200, 0615) and the limit on his order is 3 g/day because AST is 78, so the next dose is not before 1400.

Any two sleep measures: cluster care and turns, lights dimmed, door closed, noise reduced, earplugs offered, pre-medicate before turns. After oxycodone plus gabapentin: check RASS (hold for RASS -2 or lower), respiratory rate and SpO2, and reassess pain 30-60 minutes later.

items.title: Delirium and Alcohol Withdrawal Watch
items.prompt: His drinking history and an ethanol level of 42 mg/dL at 0240 on Monday were charted. Sedation is off, so days 2 to 4 after the last drink are the highest-risk window. (a) Name the four features of the CAM-ICU and say what makes it positive; what are his CAM-ICU and RASS results on this shift? (b) List four signs of alcohol withdrawal or delirium tremens you would look for and which vital signs would change first. (c) Three non-drug actions that prevent delirium tonight. (d) If he became agitated and tremulous at 0400, what would you do first and what would you ask the provider (look at what he was told to avoid)?
items.where: Flowsheets > Neuro (CAM-ICU, RASS); Chart Review > H&P (social history) and Notes; Lab Results (Toxicology); MAR (thiamine and folic acid); Pharmacy Transfer Medication Reconciliation

elements.t: CAM-ICU: (1) acute onset or fluctuating mental status, (2) inattention, (3) altered level of consciousness (RASS not 0), (4) disorganized thinking. Positive = features 1 AND 2 plus either 3 or 4. His CAM-ICU is negative at 2000, 0000 and 0400 with RASS 0 (alert and calm), and negative at 1200 and 1600 Wednesday.

Any four signs: tremor, sweating, tachycardia, hypertension, fever, nausea, anxiety/agitation, insomnia, hallucinations, disorientation, seizure; heart rate and blood pressure rise first (HR 82-89 and MAP 79-82 now).

Any three: sleep protection/clustering care, lights and day-night cycle, reorientation, glasses/family contact and phone call, early mobilization, pain control, avoid benzodiazepines and extra sedatives, treat constipation, avoid restraints; thiamine and folic acid daily.

Stay with him and check safety, vital signs, glucose, pain, bladder (Foley out), oxygen, then CAM-ICU/RASS and CIWA-type withdrawal scoring (he can talk now); notify the provider (SBAR). Question: benzodiazepines (lorazepam) are on the list to avoid because of delirium; ask what the withdrawal order would be, and about thiamine before glucose.

items.title: Pip-Tazo to Cefazolin
items.prompt: The last pip-tazo dose is given at 0030 and cefazolin 2 g IV is given at 0610. (a) Compare the two drugs for this patient: what did the blood and wound cultures grow, which drug is the best choice for it, and give TWO reasons for de-escalating from pip-tazo (look at the pharmacy and ID notes and the allergy list). (b) Pip-tazo is an extended infusion: how long does the 0030 dose run? How long is the cefazolin infusion on the order, and what rate in mL/h gives 2 g in 100 mL over that time? (c) Write the next two cefazolin times, and name two things you check before and after the first dose.
items.where: Orders (cefazolin, piperacillin-tazobactam); MAR; Lab Results (Microbiology); Chart Review > Notes (Pharmacy Stewardship Note, Burn Surgery Note); Allergies

elements.t: Blood cultures (2 of 4 bottles) and wound culture: MSSA; wound final heavy MSSA susceptible to cefazolin, nafcillin, clindamycin, TMP-SMX (resistant to penicillin); tracheal aspirate normal flora, urine no growth. Cefazolin, a first-generation cephalosporin, is a first-line, targeted drug for MSSA bacteremia and is better than vancomycin for MSSA.

Any two reasons for de-escalation: pip-tazo is broad-spectrum and no Gram-negative or anaerobic organism was found, so narrowing lowers the risk of resistance and C. difficile; narrower, targeted therapy is as good or better for MSSA; less nephrotoxicity (creatinine peaked at 1.4 on vancomycin plus pip-tazo); fewer interactions; stewardship/ID recommendation. Allergies: none known, so a cephalosporin is safe.
Pip-tazo runs over 4 hours (0030 to about 0430). Cefazolin order: infuse over 30 minutes; 100 mL / 0.5 h = 200 mL/h.

Next doses 1410 and 2210 (q8h from 0610). Check the allergy list and ask about prior reactions (none known); watch for rash, itching, hives, wheeze or low BP during and after the infusion, for diarrhea (C. difficile) later, and the creatinine; flush the line before and after and do not mix with other drugs.

items.title: Three Treatments That Stopped Overnight
items.prompt: Three supports were stopped or weaned during the night. For each one, write when and how it stopped, what the chart showed afterward (look at the 0300 and 0500 vital signs and the notes), and what you watch for next.
items.where: MAR (hydrocortisone, dexmedetomidine); Orders; Flowsheets > Vital Signs and Respiratory; Notes 0315 and 0520
cols: When it stopped / how it was tapered
What the chart showed afterward and what you watch for

elements.t: Hydrocortisone: 50 mg q6h from Tue 2030 (3 doses: 2030, 0230, 0830), then 25 mg q6h from Wed 1430 (1430, 2030, 0230); the 0230 dose was the last and the order ended at 0600 (no further dose). Afterward BP 114/66 (MAP 82) and 112/64 at 0500, HR 82. Watch for low blood pressure, weakness, fever returning, and glucose falling (less insulin resistance).

Dexmedetomidine 0.4 mcg/kg/h since Wed 1100, off at 0300. Afterward RASS 0, calm, HR 84 then 82, BP 114/66, no rebound tachycardia or hypertension, observed for 4 hours. Watch for rebound (tachycardia, hypertension, agitation), withdrawal signs and sleep, since it also masks withdrawal signs.

Oxygen: 2 L/min nasal cannula weaned to room air at 0300; SpO2 96% at 0300 and 0500, RR 18-19, lungs clear; chest x-ray at 0520 clear. Check SpO2 at rest and with turning every hour; resume oxygen for SpO2 under 92%; incentive spirometry.

items.title: The Three-Day Trend Graph
items.prompt: Study the graph of temperature, WBC, procalcitonin and creatinine for the whole stay (from the chart). Use the 0430 values on Thursday (WBC 11.2, creatinine 1.0, procalcitonin 2.1). (a) For each of the four lines, state the peak value and when it happened, and the latest value. (b) What does the graph show about the infection and about his kidneys? (c) At what time did he turn the corner, and why do the lab lines peak AFTER the temperature does? (d) What must the Med-Surg team keep watching? Give three things from the graph and the chart.
items.where: Figure below; Lab Results (WBC, Procalcitonin, Creatinine); Flowsheets > Vital Signs (Temperature); Notes (ICU Transfer Summary)

images.caption: Figure: Temperature, WBC, procalcitonin and creatinine, Monday 0700 to Thursday 0700 (dotted line = 100.4 F).

elements.t: Temperature peak 102.4 F at Tue 1930 (then falls to 100.4 by Wed 0400 and below it from 0500, 98.8 at Thu 0500; the last point on the graph is 98.5 at Thu 0700, accept 98.5-98.8). WBC peak 21.8 at Tue 2100 (now 11.2). Procalcitonin 4.8 (Tue 1600), peak 9.6 at Wed 0400, 6.1, now 2.1 at Thu 0430. Creatinine 1.1 baseline, 1.3 Tue 2300, peak 1.4 Wed 0500, 1.2, now 1.0 (admission 0.9). (Accept +/- a few hours.)

Infection: a burn wound sepsis (MSSA bacteremia) shown by the fever, leukocytosis and rising procalcitonin that are now clearly resolving (WBC and PCT falling). Kidneys: creatinine rose 1.1 to 1.4 (a mild acute kidney injury from septic shock, vancomycin plus pip-tazo, and low BP) and has recovered to 1.0, near baseline; urine output stayed adequate.

Turning point: the temperature peaked about Tuesday 1930 and the WBC at 2100, about 3 to 4.5 hours after antibiotics (pip-tazo 1630, vancomycin 1645), fluids and norepinephrine (1730); lactate fell 4.1 to 2.6 (2230); norepinephrine was off at Wed 0430. Procalcitonin and creatinine lag behind: PCT rises for 12-24 hours and falls slowly, and the creatinine reflects kidney damage that heals over a day or two; so they peak on Wednesday morning even though the patient was already improving.

Any three: a fever of 101.5 F or higher, HR over 120 or MAP under 65 (call the provider); WBC and procalcitonin must keep falling (PCT 2.1 is still above normal); creatinine/urine output after the Foley is out and with cefazolin and mafenide (BMP daily, bicarbonate); repeat blood cultures (final at 5 days); the wound for purulence, odor, spreading erythema beyond the marked line; the central line site; hydrocortisone stopped (BP).

items.title: The Arterial Line and the Foley Come Out at 0500
items.prompt: Read the 0520 nursing note. (a) Describe how you remove the left radial arterial line, how long you hold pressure (and why that could be longer in some patients), and what you check in the left hand and the site afterward and when. Which arm is used for the blood pressure now? (b) The Foley comes out at 0500: what is the target time for the first void, what do you do if he does not void, and what is his urine output goal in mL/h (0.5 mL/kg/h at 82 kg)? (c) Give two CAUTI prevention measures for the catheter days and one reason this one was removed now.
items.where: Chart Review > Notes (Nursing Note 0520); Orders (Foley care and necessity review); Devices; Lab Results (platelets, INR)

elements.t: Arterial line: wash hands and wear gloves, explain, stop the transducer/pressure bag, remove the dressing and securement, withdraw the catheter and immediately apply firm direct pressure for 5 minutes (longer if on anticoagulants or low platelets/high INR; his platelets are 186, INR 1.1, on SQ heparin), check that the catheter is intact, apply an occlusive dressing.

After removal: check the left hand for color, warmth, capillary refill (under 2 seconds), radial pulse, sensation and movement, and the site for bleeding or hematoma at 15 and 60 minutes (then per routine); BP is now by cuff on the LEFT arm (the right arm is burned and splinted).

Void within 6 hours of removal (by 1100); if no void by then or if he has suprapubic fullness/discomfort, do a bladder scan and call the provider for straight cath/orders; encourage fluids, urinal at bedside, record every void; goal 0.5 mL/kg/h x 82 kg = 41 mL/h (accept 30-41 mL/h with the reasoning; the burn surgery note asks for a call if UOP is under 30 mL/h).

Any two CAUTI measures: closed drainage system, bag below the bladder and off the floor, securement device, catheter care each shift, daily necessity review, hand hygiene. Removed now because the resuscitation is over and hourly urine output is no longer needed (day 4 of the catheter).

items.title: The Central Line on Line Day 4
items.prompt: The left IJ central line stays after the arterial line, the PIV and the Foley are gone. (a) Count the line day (look at the Devices page) and explain why ID allowed it to stay even though he had bacteremia. (b) Give three CLABSI-prevention actions you do on this line every shift. (c) What is the one question you would ask the provider to get the line out sooner?
items.where: Flowsheets > Devices and Lines; Orders (Central line care); Notes (Nursing Note 0520, ICU Transfer Summary)

elements.t: Placed Mon 11/02 0345: Mon = day 1, so Thursday is line day 4. It stays because the repeat blood cultures (Wed 1600) show no growth so far (no growth to date at about 12 hours, preliminary); ID says remove it only if they turn positive; it is also his only IV access now.

Any three: assess the site and dressing each shift (clean, dry, intact, dated chlorhexidine dressing); scrub the hub for 15 seconds before every access; minimize entries; change tubing per policy; dressing change every 7 days or if soiled; daily necessity review; hand hygiene; report fever, chills or site drainage and culture per order.

Ask: now that he is off vasopressors and eating, can we place a peripheral IV and remove the central line, or what result tells us it is safe to remove it (repeat cultures final at 5 days)? A new PIV is needed on arrival.

items.title: Is He Ready to Transfer?
items.prompt: The transfer to Med-Surg 2 East is planned for 0700. For each criterion, write the chart value or time that proves it is met (with the actual number of hours where asked), and in the last row state your decision (ready or not ready) and one concern you would still hand off.
items.where: Flowsheets (Vital Signs, I&O); MAR (norepinephrine); Devices (ETT); Notes (Burn Surgery Transfer Note, Case Management Transfer Note)
cols: Evidence from the chart (values and times)

key.answer: Each of rows 1-7 is 0.125 (criterion correctly evidenced), row 8 (decision and concern) 0.375.

elements.t: Off pressors more than 24 h: norepinephrine off Wed 0430, so 26.5 hours at 0700 (about 25.5 h at 0600); nothing vasoactive running.
Extubated more than 20 h: ETT out Wed 1045, so 20 h 15 min at 0700 (19 h at 0600; the 20-hour mark is 0645); no stridor, voice hoarse but improving.
Urine output adequate: 52-63 mL/h each hour from 1900 to 0500 (0.63-0.77 mL/kg/h) against the 41 mL/h goal.
Hemodynamics stable: HR 82-89, BP 110-114/63-66, MAP 79-82 (1900 to 0500), no pressors, lactate 1.5 (Wed 0500), afebrile 98.7-99.0 F.
Pain controlled on oral meds: 3/10 at rest on oral acetaminophen, gabapentin and oxycodone; no IV hydromorphone since Wed 1345.
Room air: since 0300, SpO2 96% (0300 and 0500), RR 18-19; chest x-ray (0520) clear.
Burn team agrees: Dr. Okafor (0600 note) and Dr. Brandt approved the transfer; case management note 0545 confirms the bed.

Decision: ready (all seven criteria met, with strong trends). One concern: no peripheral IV (central line only), first void after Foley removal is pending (by 1100), withdrawal/delirium watch after dexmedetomidine, glucose off steroids, OR Friday. A student who says "not ready" must name a criterion that is not met.

items.title: Fall Risk and Mobility After the Lines Are Out
items.prompt: The arterial line and Foley are out, he is on gabapentin and oxycodone and his right arm is splinted. Which actions are correct for the rest of this shift and the handoff?
items.where: Orders (Fall precautions, Out of bed to chair); Flowsheets > Safety and Mobility; PT note 1520; Pharmacy Transfer Medication Reconciliation
options: Keep the bed low, the bed alarm on, the call light in reach and non-skid socks on.
Assist x2 with a gait belt for any transfer to the chair or bathroom; the right arm stays elevated/splinted.
Offer the urinal and a toileting schedule, since he will have an urge to void without the Foley and may get up alone.
Let him walk to the bathroom alone now that the lines are out, because he is alert and oriented.
Hold the oxycodone and gabapentin all day so that he is less sleepy.
Turn the bed alarm off because he is oriented x4 and CAM-ICU negative.
Teach him to call before getting up, and have him dangle at the edge of the bed before standing (he had mild dizziness when he first dangled at the edge of the bed on Wednesday).
Apply a soft wrist restraint to keep him in bed.
Hand off the fall risk and the PT/OT plan to the Med-Surg nurse.

answer: Keep the bed low, the bed alarm on...
Assist x2 with a gait belt...
Offer the urinal and a toileting schedule...
Teach him to call before getting up, and have him dangle...
Hand off the fall risk and the PT/OT plan...
key.rules: 0.15 per correct option selected; subtract 0.15 for each wrong option (not below 0). Wrong options: walking alone (fall precautions need assist x2); holding all pain/neuropathic medicine (pain control is a transfer criterion; give and check RASS instead); alarm off (alarm and precautions continue); restraint (no order, extubated, calm and oriented, not indicated).

items.title: Night I&O Totals
items.prompt: Open Intake/Output and read the line "Night shift 11/04 1900 to 11/05 0700". (a) Write the intake, output and net. Compute his average urine output in mL/h and in mL/kg/h (82 kg) over the 12 hours. (b) Compare this night with the night before (11/03 1900 to 11/04 0700) and say what the change means for his fluid status. (c) His weight is 89.8 kg this morning and 82 kg on admission: what does that tell you, and how will you track output now that the Foley is out?
items.where: Flowsheets > Intake/Output (shift totals); Flowsheets > Cardiac (daily weight)

images.caption: Figure: the Totals section of Intake/Output as displayed in the EHR at 0700 Thursday.

elements.t: Night shift: intake 1,257 mL, output 638 mL, net +619 mL (as the flowsheet shows). 638 / 12 = about 53 mL/h; 53 / 82 = about 0.65 mL/kg/h (accept 0.6-0.7), above the 0.5 mL/kg/h (41 mL/h) goal. Accept 53-58 mL/h (0.65-0.71 mL/kg/h) if the student divides by the 11 hourly rows or uses the hourly values.

Previous night: 4,160 in, 803 out, +3,357. The net fell from +3,357 to +619 because the resuscitation fluids and albumin are finished (only the saline carrier and oral intake now); the capillary leak is over and the body is now holding less fluid; he is turning from fluid loading to fluid shifting back (edema 1-2+ and decreasing).

Weight is up 7.8 kg from admission: the extra water is in the tissues (edema), not new tissue, and should come off as the leak closes; track by the daily weight and edema. Without the Foley: measure each void in a urinal/hat, record the time and volume, bladder scan if no void by 6 hours, and keep intake and output charting.

items.title: The Final Handoff: Transfer SBAR to Med-Surg
items.prompt: It is 0650 on Thursday 11/05. Write your SBAR transfer handoff to C. Pruitt, RN (Med-Surg 2 East, burn step-down). Use real numbers and include: the burn infection signs to watch, central line day, the cefazolin schedule, what is still pending, the pain plan, mobility, Friday's OR and the NPO time, and the family contacts. Mention one safety item for the first hours after arrival.
items.where: Everything you read and charted this shift; Orders; MAR; Lab Results; Notes (Burn Surgery Transfer Note, ICU Transfer Summary, Case Management Note, Pharmacy Reconciliation)

elements.t: Situation: Marcus Delaney, 34 M, MRN SIM-40101, Full Code, NKDA, contact precautions, transferring from BICU-6 to 2 East at 0700; stable: T 98.8, HR 82, BP 112/64, RR 18, SpO2 96% on room air, pain 3/10, RASS 0, CAM-ICU negative.

Background: house fire 11/02, 22% TBSA (right arm, chest, face/neck; about 8% full-thickness) with grade 2 inhalation injury; intubated 0250 Mon to 1045 Wed; right forearm escharotomy; Parkland done; Tuesday MSSA burn wound sepsis with bacteremia, norepinephrine 1730 Tue to 0430 Wed, hydrocortisone stopped (last dose 0230); vancomycin stopped Wed 1530; pip-tazo last dose 0030.

Assessment: WBC 11.2, creatinine 1.0, procalcitonin 2.1, platelets 186, K 4.3 (0430); glucose 141; urine output 52-65 mL/h, night I&O +619; wounds: mafenide soaks q8h (0930, 1730, 0130), erythema inside the marked line, no purulence or odor; right hand Doppler present; left IJ central line day 4 (placed Mon 0345), site clean, A-line and Foley removed 0500 (first void by 1100), no PIV so a new one is needed; eating about half of soft diet; weight 89.8 kg.

Recommendations: watch for burn wound infection (purulent drainage, foul odor, spreading erythema past the marker, new dark/violaceous areas or eschar change, more pain) and sepsis (T 101.5 F or higher, HR over 120, MAP under 65, UOP under 30 mL/h) and call Dr. Okafor; cefazolin 2 g IV q8h next at 1410 and 2210 (over 30 min); pending: final blood culture susceptibilities, repeat blood cultures from Wed 1600 (final at 5 days; no growth to date at about 12 h), wound biopsy histology and quantitative culture (the wound culture final resulted at 0600: MSSA, cefazolin-susceptible); pain: acetaminophen 1 g q8h (max 3 g/day), gabapentin 300 mg q8h, oxycodone 5-10 mg q4h PRN 30-45 min before soaks, hydromorphone 0.5 mg IV only for severe pain; mobility: assist x2, chair with PT/OT, right arm elevated and splinted, fall precautions and bed alarm; OR Friday 11/06 for excision and autografting: NPO after midnight Thursday night, consent with the patient and Jenna Whitaker, repeat type and screen this morning; family: Jenna Whitaker (partner, health care proxy, asked to be called at any hour), Linda Delaney (mother), daughter Ava age 6, K. Abara LCSW and child life.
